In summary
California voters haven’t had to make so many decisions about tax policy at the ballot since 1990. Our analysis shows voters tend to reject new taxes.
Welcome to CalMatters, the only nonprofit newsroom devoted solely to covering issues that affect all Californians. Sign up for WhatMatters (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/whatmatters) to receive the latest news and commentary on the most important issues in the Golden State.
California voters will soon be asked whether they want to keep taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) the incomes of the rich.
And they’ll be asked whether to start taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) the accumulated wealth of the even richer.
Wait, there’s more. They’ll also get to weigh in on whether we should ban wealth taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/) altogether, subject the money raised by future taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) to a state spending cap and make it harder for voters to pass certain local taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/).
That doesn’t include any of the other propositions on the November ballot that are likely to affect the state budget. Nor does it include the roughly 300 (https://www.caltax.org/elections/local-tax-elections/2026-Local-Elections.pdf?_gl=1*pjll0w*_ga*NTYyOTYwNzgyLjE3NzYyODUwNTE.*_ga_RR9B893WL0*czE3OTA3MjI1MTEkbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGo0MyRsMCRoMA..*_ga_98RV0P0X7N*czE3OTA3MjI1MDckbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGozOSRsMCRoMA..) tax and bond measures that will be popping up in local elections across the state.
And you thought tax season only came in April.
With 14 measures in total, the 2026 California ballot (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) is a busy one. Voters haven’t been presented with this many choices in a decade. It’s an especially active year for tax-related measures — those that hike taxes, cut them, introduce new ones, jettison old ones or change the rules by which taxes are approved and enacted.
Five of those are on the ballot this time around, the most since 1990.
Altogether they have the potential to reshape the state’s finances, beef up or starve some of our largest public spending programs, change the rules around taxation and — if opponents of the proposed wealth tax (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) are to be believed — trigger a Randian exodus of the state’s wellest-to-do.
The ‘black hole’ on the ballot
Though five tax measures are on the ballot, voters are really just seeing three big questions.
The first: Should California be the first state in the nation to introduce a wealth tax?
That question is “the black hole into which all political energy is going right now,” said Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a group that advocates for low taxes.

Three measures — Propositions 40, 41 and 42 — provide opposing answers.
Prop. 40 would slap every Californian with a net worth of at least $1 billion (all approximately 200 of them) with a one-time 5% tax on their wealth, excluding real estate and retirement accounts.
This isn’t an income tax, which skims off a share of a person’s earnings, but a tax on the assessed, unrealized value of investments. Think of this like the property tax that homeowners pay on their houses, except it applies to stocks, bonds, business shares, Bugattis and the occasional machine gun collection (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/#:~:text=machine%20gun%20collection).
A sign displayed at the Billionaire Tax Now booth at the 2026 California Democratic Party State Convention in San Francisco on Feb. 21, 2026. Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that the measure has the potential to raise tens of billions of dollars. Almost all of it would be set aside for the state’s public health insurance programs, which are bracing for dramatic federal cuts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/medi-cal-the-cut-healthcare-threatened/).
That’s assuming the measure passes and survives the blizzard of inevitable legal challenges (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/07/31/opinion-why-flawed-wealth-tax-could-backfire-on-california/). Though a number of countries (https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/eu/wealth-taxes-europe/) have introduced wealth taxes at either the national or regional level, California’s would be the first in the United States.
No surprise, many of the state’s billionaires are pushing back hard. They’re doing that in the usual way, with literally hundreds of millions of dollars in campaign spending. But they’re also doing it with two additional measures on the ballot itself. Prop. 41 would, among other things (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/), ban the state from collecting taxes that circumvent a 1970s state spending limit (https://calmatters.org/politics/2021/05/newsom-tax-rebate/), which Prop. 40 is written to do.
Prop. 42 would ban new taxes on financial assets, private businesses and most other forms of wealth outright — an explicit reversal of Prop. 40.
If both the wealth tax and either of the countermeasures are approved by the voters, the one with the higher vote tally becomes law. That’s why the wealth tax could go down in defeat even if a majority of voters support it (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/).
But voters shouldn’t think of Props. 41 and 42 as mere “no” votes on Prop. 40, said Kayla Kitson, a tax policy analyst at the California Budget & Policy Center, a left-leaning think tank. Prop. 41 would also require the state’s auditor to conduct a “pre-election” analysis of any program set to be funded by a future tax measure and then make recommendations on how to cut costs by 10%.
Beyond banning future wealth taxes, Prop. 42 would also prevent future taxes from applying retroactively before a tax is approved. That could remove the state’s ability to keep people or businesses from avoiding a tax they know is coming, said Kitson.
Two more tax questions
The other two tax measures have nothing to do with the wealth tax. One would make permanent a boosted income tax rate for higher earners. The other would make it harder for local governments to raise certain taxes in the future.
The high-earner tax is the third, and possibly final, installment in a decade-long electoral trilogy.
First proposed by former Gov. Jerry Brown as a temporary (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2308&context=ca_ballot_props) solution to fund education in the fiscal hangover of the Great Recession, the measure sticks a higher tax bracket on the state’s top 2% of earners (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)). Re-authorized by voters in 2016, the tax has (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)) generated between $5 billion and $16 billion annually (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/). Most of that money has gone to schools.
The tax expires in 2030, which is why the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest K-12 public school educators’ union, was eager to put its permanent renewal on the ballot this year. If it fails, the union will have two more chances.
Hence, Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/), which would make the boosted tax rates for individually earned income above $360,000 per year a perpetual part of the state’s tax code.
Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/)’s backstory also goes back nearly a decade.
The measure would hike the share of votes needed to pass certain local taxes. Specifically, these are taxes that raise money for a specific program (https://debtguide-api.treasurer.ca.gov/guide-pages/chapter-1-legally-incurring-debt-state-law-restrictions-on-public-agency-debt-and-revenues/1-4-local-government-revenue-sources-security-for-and-repayment-of-debt/1-4-6-special-taxes) or purpose and that are placed on the ballot by citizen signature-gathering efforts, as opposed to local elected officials. If Prop. 43 passes, this very particular type of tax would need the support of at least two-thirds of local voters.
Business groups and anti-tax advocates have been wanting to put some version of Prop. 43 on the ballot since 2017 (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) when the state Supreme Court ruled that so-called citizen-initiated special taxes only need a simple majority of the vote to pass. The anti-tax advocates got close two years ago, but were stymied by another court ruling (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/). This year, the measure finally made it, but only after negotiations with the Democrats (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/) in the Legislature pared it down, applying the rule to future taxes only.
California tax measures tend to fail
This all makes for a tremendously confusing voting experience for most Californians.
That’s probably bad news for the supporters of these measures, since uncertain voters tend to err on the side of “no,” said Mark Baldassare, survey director at the Public Policy Institute of California.
“When voters aren’t sure how to proceed, staying with the status quo and letting someone else decide at a later date is a safe bet,” he said.
That may partly explain why tax measures, which are inherently complicated and tend to come with unpredictable consequences, fare especially poorly on the ballot. Since 2000, a solid majority (57%) of non-tax ballot measures have passed compared to a mere third of tax propositions.
The sheer number of open questions (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) surrounding the proposed wealth tax (Is it constitutional? Can the state effectively implement it? Will all the billionaires flee to Florida?) puts it on shakier footing with an electorate that tends to reject uncertainty, said Baldassare. A narrow majority of 52% percent of likely voters said they supported the measure in a recent PPIC poll.
The tax on high earners in Prop. 3, may face better odds because it makes permanent an existing tax rather than introducing a new one. In the same poll, 58% of likely voters indicated that they would support the measure.
“When people see the words ‘renew’ or ‘extend’ it gives them a sense that this is the status quo, we’re not being asked to make a change here,” he said.
But Prop. 3’s backers shouldn’t take too much comfort in that. Support for propositions tend to decline (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2019/10/ballot-california-polling-trend-slump-fact-check-myth-data/) as Election Day approaches. The sheer number of tax measures on offer could also inflict voters with “tax fatigue” leading them to vote “no” across the board, said Baldassare.
Then there’s the general political vibe.
Earlier this year, PPIC asked a sample of Californians whether they preferred lower taxes and fewer services or higher taxes and more services.
Fifty-five percent said they’d prefer the lower tax bill (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/).
For the record: An earlier version of this article misstated the last time voters were presented with five or more tax-related measures on the same California ballot. The most recent year was 1990, not 1994.

Real estate tax-cut proposal pulled from ballot in last-minute deal
by
Ben Christopher (https://calmatters.org/author/ben-christopher/)

In summary
The final deal puts a stripped-down tax-cut measure to voters in November but doesn’t touch real-estate transfer taxes.
Welcome to CalMatters, the only nonprofit newsroom devoted solely to covering issues that affect all Californians. Sign up for WhatMatters (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/whatmatters) to receive the latest news and commentary on the most important issues in the Golden State.
A controversial tax-chopping ballot measure was pulled from California’s November ballot in a last-minute compromise that left many legislative Democrats feeling put out.
The sudden change of electoral fortunes came after a week of frantic backroom haggling by the Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office, state legislative leaders, housing advocates, unions and business interests to convince the proposition’s sponsor to withdraw it before Thursday’s deadline.
The now-abandoned proposition to cap real estate taxes and make it harder for local governments to raise other revenues was sponsored by the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a longstanding anti-tax advocacy group.
In exchange for pulling the measure, the governor’s office and legislative leaders agreed to put a different constitutional amendment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22) on the ballot that would raise the share of votes needed to pass certain local taxes.
Democrats also agreed to remove another constitutional amendment (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) from the ballot that would have made certain tax-limiting measures much harder to pass.
Jon Coupal, president of the taxpayers association, said he was as surprised as anyone by the 11th-hour outcome after putting out a statement hours earlier declaring the negotiations dead and vowing to take the original measure to the ballot even as members of his own coalition were turning against him (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/06/tax-initiative-funders-flip-ballot-initiative-00975300).
But after days at an impasse, Newsom’s office “put something on the table that is pretty pleasing to us,” he said. “Which surprises me.”
A spokesperson from the governor’s office said the deal will free cities and other jurisdictions focus on priorities instead of cuts.
“With the (Jarvis measure) off the ballot, cities and counties can keep delivering the services Californians count on — from keeping teachers in classrooms and ensuring strong fire and emergency response, to providing health care for children and families,” spokesperson Tara Gallegos said.
California election law gave ballot measure sponsors until 5 p.m. on Thursday to voluntarily withdraw their measures. The outline of the new deal only emerged in the early afternoon. That gave the Legislature scant time to consider the grand bargain, discuss it in conference and then ram the changes through.
“Politics is about choices, and we often must navigate challenging decisions,” said Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat who introduced one of the compromise bills. “Big picture: the vote today protects vital resources for our local communities and it removes the greatest threat to our cities and their fiscal health.”
The deal gave Republicans a rare opportunity to celebrate in California’s Capitol. “This is a huge win for every Californian,” Bakersfield Sen. Shannon Grove (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/shannon-grove-77) said in a statement.

Why Democrats made a deal
The proposition was the kind of fiscal one-two punch to keep Democrats, local governments and other left-of-center interest groups up at night.
First, it would have limited local transfer taxes — fees on the sale of real estate — to no more than 0.055% (fifty-five cents for every $1,000 in a property’s value). Twenty-six cities, including some of the state’s largest, have levies set well above that cutoff, with Los Angeles’ mansion tax (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/), which funds affordable housing and renter assistance, maxing out at 100 times that rate.
The proposition would have also raised the share of votes needed for certain types of local taxes. Though many local tax measures in California require the support of two-thirds of voters, those placed on the ballot through signature gathering campaigns to fund specific purposes only need more than 50% (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/). The Jarvis proposition would have nixed that rule and voided any measures enacted since 2017 that didn’t meet the two-thirds requirement.
Instead, under Thursday’s deal, voters will consider the 50% rule on local tax measures alone, though it would not apply retroactively.
Though public polling (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-education-april-2026/) suggested that Howard Jarvis’s proposition faced long odds in California, lawmakers, unions and other opponents worried that voters could be persuaded to back an anti-tax measure amid heightened concerns about affordability and the cost of living. The double-barrelled tax cut would have blown a multibillion-dollar hole in municipal budgets annually, but would have saved local taxpayers just as much, according to an estimate (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0006A1%29.pdf) by the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Cities aren’t enthusiastic about the new deal, which would give voters a chance to cut off what has become a frequently used funding source for public programs.
“At a time when cities are already struggling to maintain a high quality of service in a context of high inflation, runaway costs for basic goods and services, cuts in federal funding, and stagnant sales revenue, efforts that limit the ability to raise local revenues only deepen uncertainty for local governments and the communities they serve,” Carolyn Coleman, director of the League of California Cities, said in a written statement.
Even so, the league said it does not yet have a formal position on the new measure.
The bargain also removed an especially convoluted constitutional amendment (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) from the ballot that was designed to ensnare the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association by requiring any future proposition that wanted to hike the voter threshold needed to pass a law (say, from 50% to two-thirds) to itself pass by the higher threshold.
What about transfer taxes?
Left out of the compromise is anything about transfer taxes, a topic that has dominated the public debate (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) over the proposition and provided much of the fuel for its earlier signature gathering campaign.
On Monday, Wicks, who is aligned with the pro-development “Yes In My Backyard” movement, rolled out Assembly Bill 736 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab736) as a possible legislative off-ramp. The bill would have capped transfer taxes at between 1.5% and 3%, depending on the type of tax. That’s well above the Howard Jarvis-backed cut-off, but would have been a significant rate cut for a handful of high-tax municipalities like Los Angeles, Santa Monica, Culver City, San Jose and San Francisco.
For Wicks and her YIMBY allies, the bill is seen as more than a simple electoral instrument. Pro-development groups have pointed to high transfer taxes (https://housingactioncoalition.org/news/hac-ed-homes4good-transfer-tax) as one of many impediments to the construction of much-needed housing.
The proposal also got the backing of the California Business Roundtable, a large business coalition whose members include major real estate investors and which has been bankrolling the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association’s campaign.
With the funders endorsing a legislative compromise, it seemed possible that the taxpayers association would also be willing to back the lower tax cap.
The political pressure ratcheted up even further on Wednesday. As Politico first reported, the heads of three major real estate investment firms said that they were ready to spend at least $10 million (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/06/tax-initiative-funders-flip-ballot-initiative-00975300) battling the measure if Coupal didn’t back down.
Until the final hours, it seemed like he wouldn’t.
“We’ve had lots of partners help us qualify this initiative, but we are the ultimate decider as to whether or not we proceed with our initiative,” said Jon Coupal, the association’s president told CalMatters earlier this week. “It is our intention to proceed.”
Striking a deal that could make it harder to raise new local taxes represents a long-sought policy win (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) for the taxpayer group. Capping transfer taxes appears to have been less of a priority. The Wicks bill “is floating out there which people can support or not support, it’s up to them,” he said.
But the political calculus over AB 736has changed. Even before Thursday’s deal was announced, an ideologically diverse array of interest groups had already rallied to defeat it: The California Association of Realtors, local government groups, many affordable housing developers and tenant rights advocates.
Without a proposition hanging over their head anymore, legislators aren’t likely to have much appetite to take such a difficult vote.
All eyes on LA
The transfer tax omission comes as a disappointment to many real estate interests and pro-development advocates, particularly in Los Angeles, which has been the center of the statewide debate over transfer taxes this year.
Since 2023, the city has had the among the highest transfer taxes in California in the form of Measure ULA. That policy, backed by the city’s voters, places a 4% tax on real estate sales over roughly $5 million and 5.5% on those just above $10 million. So far it’s raised more than $1.2 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) for affordable housing, renter assistance and eviction defense.
But despite the “mansion tax” moniker, the tax also applies to apartment developments, condos, commercial and industrial projects. A number of academic analyses have blamed the tax for the city’s abnormal drop in new multifamily housing construction and for reducing property tax revenue. Politically, the animosity toward Measure ULA by Los Angeles-based real estate developers and investors has provided significant fuel (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/#:~:text=along,ULA) behind the Howard Jarvis measure, the proposition’s backers have said.
“It’s crazy that poorly designed transfer taxes like Measure ULA spurred this effort, but at the end of the day, Measure ULA and other similar measures will remain untouched,” said Mott Smith, chairman of the Council of Infill Builders and prominent advocate for changing the L.A. tax.
Change may still be on the docket for Los Angeles. Earlier this month, the city council voted to put a measure on the local ballot to exempt apartment and mixed-use buildings (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/mansion-tax-housing-ballot-measure-city-council-vote-november) from the higher transfer tax within the 10 years of construction. That proposal is expected to get a final council vote next week.
The failure to address transfer taxes only reinforces the need for Los Angeles to act, said Leo Daube, a spokesperson for Councilmember Katy Yaroslavsky, who introduced the proposed change.
“If Sacramento is not going to do it, then Los Angeles should,” he said.

Welcome to CalMatters, the only nonprofit newsroom devoted solely to covering issues that affect all Californians. Sign up for WhatMatters (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/whatmatters) to receive the latest news and commentary on the most important issues in the Golden State.
A controversial tax-chopping ballot measure was pulled from California’s November ballot in a last-minute compromise that left many legislative Democrats feeling put out.
The sudden change of electoral fortunes came after a week of frantic backroom haggling by the Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office, state legislative leaders, housing advocates, unions and business interests to convince the proposition’s sponsor to withdraw it before Thursday’s deadline.
The now-abandoned proposition to cap real estate taxes and make it harder for local governments to raise other revenues was sponsored by the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a longstanding anti-tax advocacy group.
In exchange for pulling the measure, the governor’s office and legislative leaders agreed to put a different constitutional amendment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22) on the ballot that would raise the share of votes needed to pass certain local taxes.
Democrats also agreed to remove another constitutional amendment (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) from the ballot that would have made certain tax-limiting measures much harder to pass.
Jon Coupal, president of the taxpayers association, said he was as surprised as anyone by the 11th-hour outcome after putting out a statement hours earlier declaring the negotiations dead and vowing to take the original measure to the ballot even as members of his own coalition were turning against him (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/06/tax-initiative-funders-flip-ballot-initiative-00975300).
But after days at an impasse, Newsom’s office “put something on the table that is pretty pleasing to us,” he said. “Which surprises me.”
A spokesperson from the governor’s office said the deal will free cities and other jurisdictions focus on priorities instead of cuts.
“With the (Jarvis measure) off the ballot, cities and counties can keep delivering the services Californians count on — from keeping teachers in classrooms and ensuring strong fire and emergency response, to providing health care for children and families,” spokesperson Tara Gallegos said.
California election law gave ballot measure sponsors until 5 p.m. on Thursday to voluntarily withdraw their measures. The outline of the new deal only emerged in the early afternoon. That gave the Legislature scant time to consider the grand bargain, discuss it in conference and then ram the changes through.
“Politics is about choices, and we often must navigate challenging decisions,” said Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat who introduced one of the compromise bills. “Big picture: the vote today protects vital resources for our local communities and it removes the greatest threat to our cities and their fiscal health.”
The deal gave Republicans a rare opportunity to celebrate in California’s Capitol. “This is a huge win for every Californian,” Bakersfield Sen. Shannon Grove (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/shannon-grove-77) said in a statement.

Why Democrats made a deal
The proposition was the kind of fiscal one-two punch to keep Democrats, local governments and other left-of-center interest groups up at night.
First, it would have limited local transfer taxes — fees on the sale of real estate — to no more than 0.055% (fifty-five cents for every $1,000 in a property’s value). Twenty-six cities, including some of the state’s largest, have levies set well above that cutoff, with Los Angeles’ mansion tax (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/), which funds affordable housing and renter assistance, maxing out at 100 times that rate.
The proposition would have also raised the share of votes needed for certain types of local taxes. Though many local tax measures in California require the support of two-thirds of voters, those placed on the ballot through signature gathering campaigns to fund specific purposes only need more than 50% (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/). The Jarvis proposition would have nixed that rule and voided any measures enacted since 2017 that didn’t meet the two-thirds requirement.
Instead, under Thursday’s deal, voters will consider the 50% rule on local tax measures alone, though it would not apply retroactively.
Though public polling (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-education-april-2026/) suggested that Howard Jarvis’s proposition faced long odds in California, lawmakers, unions and other opponents worried that voters could be persuaded to back an anti-tax measure amid heightened concerns about affordability and the cost of living. The double-barrelled tax cut would have blown a multibillion-dollar hole in municipal budgets annually, but would have saved local taxpayers just as much, according to an estimate (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0006A1%29.pdf) by the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Cities aren’t enthusiastic about the new deal, which would give voters a chance to cut off what has become a frequently used funding source for public programs.
“At a time when cities are already struggling to maintain a high quality of service in a context of high inflation, runaway costs for basic goods and services, cuts in federal funding, and stagnant sales revenue, efforts that limit the ability to raise local revenues only deepen uncertainty for local governments and the communities they serve,” Carolyn Coleman, director of the League of California Cities, said in a written statement.
Even so, the league said it does not yet have a formal position on the new measure.
The bargain also removed an especially convoluted constitutional amendment (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) from the ballot that was designed to ensnare the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association by requiring any future proposition that wanted to hike the voter threshold needed to pass a law (say, from 50% to two-thirds) to itself pass by the higher threshold.
What about transfer taxes?
Left out of the compromise is anything about transfer taxes, a topic that has dominated the public debate (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) over the proposition and provided much of the fuel for its earlier signature gathering campaign.

The proposal also got the backing of the California Business Roundtable, a large business coalition whose members include major real estate investors and which has been bankrolling the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association’s campaign.

As Politico first reported, the heads of three major real estate investment firms said that they were ready to spend at least $10 million (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/06/tax-initiative-funders-flip-ballot-initiative-00975300) battling the measure if Coupal didn’t back down.
Until the final hours, it seemed like he wouldn’t.

Capping transfer taxes appears to have been less of a priority. The Wicks bill “is floating out there which people can support or not support, it’s up to them,” he said.

Even before Thursday’s deal was announced, an ideologically diverse array of interest groups had already rallied to defeat it: The California Association of Realtors, local government groups, many affordable housing developers and tenant rights advocates.

The transfer tax omission comes as a disappointment to many real estate interests and pro-development advocates, particularly in Los Angeles, which has been the center of the statewide debate over transfer taxes this year.
Since 2023, the city has had the among the highest transfer taxes in California in the form of Measure ULA. That policy, backed by the city’s voters, places a 4% tax on real estate sales over roughly $5 million and 5.5% on those just above $10 million. So far it’s raised more than $1.2 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) for affordable housing, renter assistance and eviction defense.

A number of academic analyses have blamed the tax for the city’s abnormal drop in new multifamily housing construction and for reducing property tax revenue. Earlier this month, the city council voted to put a measure on the local ballot to exempt apartment and mixed-use buildings (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/mansion-tax-housing-ballot-measure-city-council-vote-november) from the higher transfer tax within the 10 years of construction. That proposal is expected to get a final council vote next week.

A controversial tax-chopping ballot measure was pulled from California’s November ballot in a last-minute compromise that left many legislative Democrats feeling put out.
The sudden change of electoral fortunes came after a week of frantic backroom haggling by the Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office, state legislative leaders, housing advocates, unions and business interests to convince the proposition’s sponsor to withdraw it before Thursday’s deadline.
The now-abandoned proposition to cap real estate taxes and make it harder for local governments to raise other revenues was sponsored by the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a longstanding anti-tax advocacy group.
In exchange for pulling the measure, the governor’s office and legislative leaders agreed to put a different constitutional amendment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22) on the ballot that would raise the share of votes needed to pass certain local taxes.
Democrats also agreed to remove another constitutional amendment (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) from the ballot that would have made certain tax-limiting measures much harder to pass.
Jon Coupal, president of the taxpayers association, said he was as surprised as anyone by the 11th-hour outcome after putting out a statement hours earlier declaring the negotiations dead and vowing to take the original measure to the ballot even as members of his own coalition were turning against him (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/06/tax-initiative-funders-flip-ballot-initiative-00975300).

A spokesperson from the governor’s office said the deal will free cities and other jurisdictions focus on priorities instead of cuts.
“With the (Jarvis measure) off the ballot, cities and counties can keep delivering the services Californians count on — from keeping teachers in classrooms and ensuring strong fire and emergency response, to providing health care for children and families,” spokesperson Tara Gallegos said.
California election law gave ballot measure sponsors until 5 p.m. on Thursday to voluntarily withdraw their measures. The outline of the new deal only emerged in the early afternoon. “Politics is about choices, and we often must navigate challenging decisions,” said Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat who introduced one of the compromise bills. “Big picture: the vote today protects vital resources for our local communities and it removes the greatest threat to our cities and their fiscal health.”
The deal gave Republicans a rare opportunity to celebrate in California’s Capitol. “This is a huge win for every Californian,” Bakersfield Sen. Shannon Grove (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/shannon-grove-77) said in a statement.

- **Sponsor/proponent:** Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22 as a legislative compromise.
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association drove the underlying policy and its qualified citizen initiative.
- **On the ballot because:** The legislature placed it on the ballot by a two-thirds vote of each house on June 25, 2026, as a compromise.
In exchange, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association withdrew its already-qualified initiative (AG No. 25-0006A1).

In summary
The final deal puts a stripped-down tax-cut measure to voters in November but doesn’t touch real-estate transfer taxes.

A controversial tax-chopping ballot measure was pulled from California’s November ballot in a last-minute compromise that left many legislative Democrats feeling put out.
The sudden change of electoral fortunes came after a week of frantic backroom haggling by the Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office, state legislative leaders, housing advocates, unions and business interests to convince the proposition’s sponsor to withdraw it before Thursday’s deadline.
The now-abandoned proposition to cap real estate taxes and make it harder for local governments to raise other revenues was sponsored by the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a longstanding anti-tax advocacy group.
In exchange for pulling the measure, the governor’s office and legislative leaders agreed to put a different constitutional amendment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22) on the ballot that would raise the share of votes needed to pass certain local taxes.
Democrats also agreed to remove another constitutional amendment (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) from the ballot that would have made certain tax-limiting measures much harder to pass.
Jon Coupal, president of the taxpayers association, said he was as surprised as anyone by the 11th-hour outcome after putting out a statement hours earlier declaring the negotiations dead and vowing to take the original measure to the ballot even as members of his own coalition were turning against him (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/06/tax-initiative-funders-flip-ballot-initiative-00975300).
But after days at an impasse, Newsom’s office “put something on the table that is pretty pleasing to us,” he said. “Which surprises me.”
A spokesperson from the governor’s office said the deal will free cities and other jurisdictions focus on priorities instead of cuts.
“With the (Jarvis measure) off the ballot, cities and counties can keep delivering the services Californians count on — from keeping teachers in classrooms and ensuring strong fire and emergency response, to providing health care for children and families,” spokesperson Tara Gallegos said.
California election law gave ballot measure sponsors until 5 p.m. on Thursday to voluntarily withdraw their measures. The outline of the new deal only emerged in the early afternoon. That gave the Legislature scant time to consider the grand bargain, discuss it in conference and then ram the changes through.
“Politics is about choices, and we often must navigate challenging decisions,” said Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat who introduced one of the compromise bills. “Big picture: the vote today protects vital resources for our local communities and it removes the greatest threat to our cities and their fiscal health.”
The deal gave Republicans a rare opportunity to celebrate in California’s Capitol. “This is a huge win for every Californian,” Bakersfield Sen. Shannon Grove (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/shannon-grove-77) said in a statement.

Why Democrats made a deal
The proposition was the kind of fiscal one-two punch to keep Democrats, local governments and other left-of-center interest groups up at night.
First, it would have limited local transfer taxes — fees on the sale of real estate — to no more than 0.055% (fifty-five cents for every $1,000 in a property’s value). Twenty-six cities, including some of the state’s largest, have levies set well above that cutoff, with Los Angeles’ mansion tax (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/), which funds affordable housing and renter assistance, maxing out at 100 times that rate.
The proposition would have also raised the share of votes needed for certain types of local taxes. Though many local tax measures in California require the support of two-thirds of voters, those placed on the ballot through signature gathering campaigns to fund specific purposes only need more than 50% (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/). The Jarvis proposition would have nixed that rule and voided any measures enacted since 2017 that didn’t meet the two-thirds requirement.
Instead, under Thursday’s deal, voters will consider the 50% rule on local tax measures alone, though it would not apply retroactively.
Though public polling (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-education-april-2026/) suggested that Howard Jarvis’s proposition faced long odds in California, lawmakers, unions and other opponents worried that voters could be persuaded to back an anti-tax measure amid heightened concerns about affordability and the cost of living. The double-barrelled tax cut would have blown a multibillion-dollar hole in municipal budgets annually, but would have saved local taxpayers just as much, according to an estimate (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0006A1%29.pdf) by the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Cities aren’t enthusiastic about the new deal, which would give voters a chance to cut off what has become a frequently used funding source for public programs.
“At a time when cities are already struggling to maintain a high quality of service in a context of high inflation, runaway costs for basic goods and services, cuts in federal funding, and stagnant sales revenue, efforts that limit the ability to raise local revenues only deepen uncertainty for local governments and the communities they serve,” Carolyn Coleman, director of the League of California Cities, said in a written statement.
Even so, the league said it does not yet have a formal position on the new measure.
The bargain also removed an especially convoluted constitutional amendment (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) from the ballot that was designed to ensnare the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association by requiring any future proposition that wanted to hike the voter threshold needed to pass a law (say, from 50% to two-thirds) to itself pass by the higher threshold.
What about transfer taxes?
Left out of the compromise is anything about transfer taxes, a topic that has dominated the public debate (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) over the proposition and provided much of the fuel for its earlier signature gathering campaign.
On Monday, Wicks, who is aligned with the pro-development “Yes In My Backyard” movement, rolled out Assembly Bill 736 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab736) as a possible legislative off-ramp. The bill would have capped transfer taxes at between 1.5% and 3%, depending on the type of tax. That’s well above the Howard Jarvis-backed cut-off, but would have been a significant rate cut for a handful of high-tax municipalities like Los Angeles, Santa Monica, Culver City, San Jose and San Francisco.
For Wicks and her YIMBY allies, the bill is seen as more than a simple electoral instrument. Pro-development groups have pointed to high transfer taxes (https://housingactioncoalition.org/news/hac-ed-homes4good-transfer-tax) as one of many impediments to the construction of much-needed housing.
The proposal also got the backing of the California Business Roundtable, a large business coalition whose members include major real estate investors and which has been bankrolling the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association’s campaign.
With the funders endorsing a legislative compromise, it seemed possible that the taxpayers association would also be willing to back the lower tax cap.
The political pressure ratcheted up even further on Wednesday. As Politico first reported, the heads of three major real estate investment firms said that they were ready to spend at least $10 million (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/06/tax-initiative-funders-flip-ballot-initiative-00975300) battling the measure if Coupal didn’t back down.
Until the final hours, it seemed like he wouldn’t.
“We’ve had lots of partners help us qualify this initiative, but we are the ultimate decider as to whether or not we proceed with our initiative,” said Jon Coupal, the association’s president told CalMatters earlier this week. “It is our intention to proceed.”
Striking a deal that could make it harder to raise new local taxes represents a long-sought policy win (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) for the taxpayer group. Capping transfer taxes appears to have been less of a priority. The Wicks bill “is floating out there which people can support or not support, it’s up to them,” he said.
But the political calculus over AB 736has changed. Even before Thursday’s deal was announced, an ideologically diverse array of interest groups had already rallied to defeat it: The California Association of Realtors, local government groups, many affordable housing developers and tenant rights advocates.
Without a proposition hanging over their head anymore, legislators aren’t likely to have much appetite to take such a difficult vote.
All eyes on LA
The transfer tax omission comes as a disappointment to many real estate interests and pro-development advocates, particularly in Los Angeles, which has been the center of the statewide debate over transfer taxes this year.
Since 2023, the city has had the among the highest transfer taxes in California in the form of Measure ULA. That policy, backed by the city’s voters, places a 4% tax on real estate sales over roughly $5 million and 5.5% on those just above $10 million. So far it’s raised more than $1.2 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) for affordable housing, renter assistance and eviction defense.
But despite the “mansion tax” moniker, the tax also applies to apartment developments, condos, commercial and industrial projects. A number of academic analyses have blamed the tax for the city’s abnormal drop in new multifamily housing construction and for reducing property tax revenue. Politically, the animosity toward Measure ULA by Los Angeles-based real estate developers and investors has provided significant fuel (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/#:~:text=along,ULA) behind the Howard Jarvis measure, the proposition’s backers have said.
“It’s crazy that poorly designed transfer taxes like Measure ULA spurred this effort, but at the end of the day, Measure ULA and other similar measures will remain untouched,” said Mott Smith, chairman of the Council of Infill Builders and prominent advocate for changing the L.A. tax.
Change may still be on the docket for Los Angeles. Earlier this month, the city council voted to put a measure on the local ballot to exempt apartment and mixed-use buildings (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/mansion-tax-housing-ballot-measure-city-council-vote-november) from the higher transfer tax within the 10 years of construction. That proposal is expected to get a final council vote next week.
The failure to address transfer taxes only reinforces the need for Los Angeles to act, said Leo Daube, a spokesperson for Councilmember Katy Yaroslavsky, who introduced the proposed change.
“If Sacramento is not going to do it, then Los Angeles should,” he said.

I authored ACA 22 not because I wanted it to become law – but because it was the only path left to get the more dangerous initiative off the ballot before time ran out.
...

PROP 43: Two-Thirds Vote for Local Special Taxes
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%2043.pdf)
Research
Quick Facts
Key Questions
Risks & Benefits
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
​​​​​​ Official ballot title: “Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.”
Type: Legislative constitutional amendment (Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22, Resolution Chapter 132, filed with the secretary of state June 25, 2026)
A vote YES means: New, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters through the initiative power would need a two-thirds vote to pass, the same threshold already required when a city council or county board places a special tax on the ballot. Local governments and their voters also could not impose ad valorem property taxes beyond the limits already in the state constitution.
A vote NO means: Certain local special taxes could continue to be approved by a simple majority vote when placed on the ballot by citizen initiative.
Sponsor/proponent: Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22 as a legislative compromise. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association drove the underlying policy and its qualified citizen initiative.
On the ballot because: The legislature placed it on the ballot by a two-thirds vote of each house on June 25, 2026, as a compromise. In exchange, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association withdrew its already-qualified initiative (AG No. 25-0006A1).
Full legal text: ACA 22, Resolution Chapter 132, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22)
LAO analysis: Legislative Analyst’s Office, Proposition 43 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 43 would raise the vote threshold for one specific path to a new local tax. Today, when a city council or county board of supervisors asks voters to approve a special tax, meaning a tax earmarked for a specific purpose, that tax needs a two-thirds vote to pass. That requirement traces to Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996. A separate path exists. When voters themselves place a special tax on the ballot through the citizen initiative, a series of court decisions has allowed that tax to pass with a simple majority. Proposition 43 would close that gap. Beginning January 1, 2027, a voter-initiated local special tax would need the same two-thirds vote as a government-sponsored one.
The measure carries a second provision that has drawn less attention. It also bars a local government, including its electorate acting by initiative, from imposing ad valorem taxes on real property beyond the 1 percent rate that Proposition 13 already allows. This extends the existing constitutional limit so that it cannot be worked around through the initiative power.
The Legislative Analyst’s Office frames the practical effect plainly. By raising the bar for these taxes, the measure makes it harder for local governments to raise certain revenues, so local tax collections could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The office adds that the actual impact is unknown and would depend on future choices by voters and local officials.
2. The legal language
Full text: ACA 22, “Local Taxes: Limitation,” Resolution Chapter 132, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22) (filed with the secretary of state June 25, 2026)
Key language:
“Beginning on January 1, 2027, and notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax, except as provided in Section 4 of this article, subdivision (d) of Section 2 of Article XIII C, and paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D, unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote.” [1, Sec. 4.5(a)]
What it amends: Adds Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution, the article created by Proposition 13. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal it on its own. The phrase “including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power” is the operative change, since it applies the two-thirds requirement to citizen initiatives, which recent court rulings had exempted.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22, but she did so as the vehicle for a negotiated deal rather than as a personal cause, and she has since said she opposes the measure. The policy behind it belongs to the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and its president, Jon Coupal, who had qualified a broader citizen initiative and agreed to pull it once the legislature placed this narrower version on the ballot. Opposition comes from transit, housing, and local government advocates who rely on majority-vote initiatives to fund services.
What? A two-thirds vote requirement for voter-initiated local special taxes, plus a bar on using the initiative power to impose ad valorem property taxes beyond the existing 1 percent limit.
Where? Statewide in effect, but it governs local taxes, so its bite is felt in the cities, counties, and special districts where citizen tax initiatives appear.
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. The requirement applies to taxes beginning January 1, 2027.
Why? Supporters argue that a special tax is a special tax no matter who puts it on the ballot, and that letting initiatives pass earmarked taxes by a simple majority is an end run around a taxpayer protection that has stood since Proposition 13. Opponents argue that the citizen initiative is a core democratic tool and that a supermajority requirement lets a minority of voters block services the majority wants.
4. Trade-offs
For roughly two decades after Proposition 218, most people assumed every local special tax needed two-thirds approval. The California Supreme Court unsettled that assumption in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017), holding that the procedural limits Proposition 218 placed on local governments do not automatically bind voters acting through the initiative. The court itself called the change modest and left the two-thirds question open. Lower courts then took the next step, upholding several citizen special taxes that had passed with a majority rather than a two-thirds vote. That line of cases is what Proposition 43 would overturn.
The trade-off is real on both sides. The measure closes what supporters see as a loophole that lets organized campaigns pass targeted taxes with less consensus than the state constitution otherwise demands. A two-thirds rule protects the minority who bear the tax, and it forces broad agreement before money is committed to a single purpose. But the same rule is a powerful brake. Supermajority requirements let roughly one-third of voters defeat what a majority supports, and the taxes that have passed by majority under the current rule are not abstractions. They have funded things like fire protection, health services, and open-space preservation in specific counties. Under Proposition 43 several of those recent measures would have failed despite winning majority support.
There is also a worthwhile point about scope. Proposition 43 is deliberately narrower than the initiative it replaced. The original Howard Jarvis measure would also have restricted certain charter-city real estate transfer taxes and would have reached backward to invalidate some taxes already in place. ACA 22 drops both of those features and applies only going forward. Voters weighing this measure are voting on the prospective threshold change and the ad valorem limit, not on the more sweeping version that was withdrawn.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
It restores a single, consistent rule. A local special tax would need two-thirds approval regardless of whether a city council or a citizen initiative places it on the ballot, ending a distinction that turned on procedure rather than substance.
It strengthens a long-standing taxpayer protection. The two-thirds requirement for earmarked local taxes has been part of California law since Proposition 13 and Proposition 218, and the measure keeps the initiative power from bypassing it.
It is prospective and narrow. Unlike the withdrawn initiative, it does not invalidate existing taxes or add new limits on real estate transfer taxes, which reduces the risk of disruptively unwinding revenue already budgeted.
It adds certainty. Litigation since Upland left the majority-versus-two-thirds question unsettled for years, and a clear constitutional rule would end that ambiguity.
Potential risks
It makes it harder to fund local services. The Legislative Analyst finds local tax revenues could be lower than they otherwise would be, though the size of the effect is unknown.
It lets a minority block a majority. A tax with 60 percent support would fail, so about one-third of voters could defeat a measure the majority favors.
It narrows a core democratic tool. The citizen initiative was designed to let voters act when their elected officials will not, and the measure raises the bar specifically for that path.
Real recent examples would have failed. Several county special taxes for fire, health, and open space passed with majorities below two-thirds and would not have survived this rule.
The ad valorem provision is easy to overlook. Most coverage focuses on the vote threshold, yet the measure also writes a real property tax limit into the constitution, and its practical reach deserves scrutiny.
6. Open questions
How many recent local special taxes actually passed with between a majority and two-thirds vote, and how much revenue statewide would have been at stake under the new rule?
Does the ad valorem provision in subdivision (b) change anything on the ground, or does it mainly codify limits that courts already enforced?
Will the narrower ACA 22 satisfy the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association over time, or does the withdrawn initiative signal a broader effort to come?
How will the measure interact with the exceptions it cross-references in Article XIII C and Article XIII D, and which taxes fall inside or outside those carve-outs?
With the author now opposed to her own measure, how will the yes and no campaigns be organized and funded?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
A special tax funds one specific thing, and the state constitution has long asked for two-thirds approval before a city or county can levy one. Should the same two-thirds rule apply when voters put that tax on the ballot themselves, or should the citizen initiative be a path to a simple-majority tax that elected officials could not pass on their own?
Ask which risk worries you more: A supermajority rule that lets one-third of voters block services the majority wants, or a majority rule that lets an organized campaign commit a community to a targeted tax with less consensus than the constitution otherwise requires?

Requires a Two-Thirds Vote to Approve Local Special Tax Initiatives
PROP
43 Purpose
Proposition 43 is a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature that would raise the
vote share required to enact special tax initiatives proposed by citizens from a simple majority
to a two-thirds majority.1
CALIFORNIA
Research Assistant: Kahani Malhotra ’27
Background
In 1978, California voters passed Proposition 13, requiring that any special tax proposed by a
local government must receive a two-thirds vote from the electorate before being enacted,2
with a special tax being defined as any tax imposed for a specific purpose rather than general
governmental need.3 In 1996, Proposition 218 further increased the power of voters to approve
taxes by requiring that any general tax imposed by a local government must receive majority
voter approval, and reaffirmed that special taxes require two-thirds voter approval.4
Two decades later, a court decision narrowed the scope of Proposition 218. In 2017, the
California Supreme Court ruled in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland that a significant
requirement for general taxes — that they be placed on the ballot during general elections —
did not apply to citizen initiatives.5 Ultimately, the court categorized taxes imposed by local
governments as different from taxes imposed by citizen initiatives.
The ruling raised an important question: Are special taxes imposed by citizen initiatives exempt
from the two-thirds vote requirement that applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local
governments? A memo from the San Francisco attorney’s office interpreting the ruling seemed
to indicate that the answer was yes.6 But the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association disagreed.
In 2018, the Association sued San Francisco for allowing two separate citizen-driven measures
to pass with a simple-majority vote rather than a supermajority vote. A judge ruled against the
Association, affirming that the special tax measures were rightfully passed by majority vote
since they were proposed by citizens.7 A state appeals court shot down the Association’s further
attempts to overturn citizen-initiated local taxes passed in 20208 and 2021.9
In 2023, the Association and the California Business Roundtable qualified an initiative10 for the
2024 ballot cycle that would have mandated any special tax initiative to require a two-thirds
majority vote regardless of whether a local government or citizens proposed it.11 But in June
2024, the California Supreme Court ruled unanimously that passage of the initiative would lead
to a “revision,” rather than an amendment, of the state constitution, “based on its far-reaching
changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained at the
state and local levels.” While amendments may be made by citizen initiatives, revisions require
“a constitutional convention and popular ratification.”12 Thus, enacting the proposal by initiative
would be unconstitutional.
In 2026, the same two organizations qualified an initiative for the 2026 general election
ballot that would have amended the state constitution to require a two-thirds majority to pass
citizen-led local special tax initiatives, alongside other tax limiting provisions.13 Following a
legislative compromise, which included the passage of ACA 22,14 the organizations withdrew the
initiative in favor of Proposition 43 being placed on this year’s ballot as a legislatively referred
constitutional amendment.15 Though ACA 22 passed nearly unanimously in the Assembly (68-2)
and Senate (35-1), its author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-14), announced on June 29 that
she was “adamantly opposed to it.16
Proposal
Proposition 43 would amend the
California Constitution to require that
citizen-driven special tax initiatives
require a two-thirds majority vote
for passage. It would add Section
4.5 to Article XIII A of the California
Constitution, detailing that any local
government — including voters
within a local government exercising
the initiative power — must obtain
a two-thirds vote to enact, extend,
or increase a special tax starting on
January 1, 2027.
The amendment also prohibits local
government and members of the
electorate from levying ad valorem
property taxes — taxes based on the
value of real estate or tangible per-
sonal property — except for certain
preapproved, dedicated property
taxes, whose terms are delineated in
the Constitution.17
Fiscal Impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s
Office (LAO) estimates that Propo-
sition 43 would reduce local govern-
ment tax revenues. The total fiscal
impact is largely unknown, however,
as it depends on future decisions by
voters and local governments.18
ROSEINSTITUTE.CMC.EDU
Supporters of Proposition 43 Include:19
• Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association20
• California Taxpayers Association
• California Small Business Association
• Family Business Association of California
• California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
• Reform California21
• California Republican Party
The proponents’ official website is “Yes on 43: Taxpayer
Protection,” https://yesonprop43.com/.
As of September 19, 2026, proponents had raised a total of
$14,856,760.22
Supporters argue that Proposition 43 would:23
• Restore the protections of Prop. 13 (1978) by closing
loopholes created by courts so that local special taxes
must be approved by two-thirds of voters.
• Make it more difficult for special interests to collude with
local governments to impose costly taxes on homeowners,
renters, and small businesses.
• Ensure that taxpayers are in charge by fully protecting their
right to vote on taxes.
• Prevent other rollbacks of Proposition 13.
SUPPORT FOR PROPOSITION 43
Opponents of Proposition 43 Include:24
• California Democratic Party25
• State Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-14)26
• Evolve California27
• Sierra Business Council
• California Professional Firefighters
• Nurse Alliance of SEIU California
• California School Employees Association
• California State Association of Counties
• League of Women Voters of California
• California Teachers Association
The opponents’ official website is “No on 43,”
https://www.noprop43ca.com/.
As of September 19, 2026, opponents had raised a total of
$4,864,393.28
Opponents argue that Proposition 43 would:29
• Threaten funding for parks, affordable housing, firefight-
ing, and other crucial local services that rely on local
revenue.30
• Make it more difficult for cities to secure future revenue
measures.31
• Make California “the hardest place in the country” to raise
local revenue.32
• Undermine majority rule by empowering a minority to
block tax measures favored by a supermajority of voters.
OPPOSITION TO PROPOSITION 43
A YES vote for Proposition 43 would increase the threshold
to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives to a two-thirds
majority vote.
A NO vote for Proposition 43 would maintain a simple majority
requirement to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives.

Bay Area officials are sounding the alarm over a lesser-known California ballot measure
By Kathryn Palmer (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/kathryn-palmer/) , Staff Writer Oct 12, 2026
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie appears alongside first responders to oppose Proposition 43 outside of Fire Station No. 5 on Oct. 7.
Weston Turtle Fudge/S.F. Chronicle
It’s not often that the supporters and opponents of a ballot measure agree on what exactly it would do, let alone describe it the same way. Yet both sides of the fight over Proposition 43 have been clear: It will make it harder to raise local taxes.
What they don’t agree on is whether it’s a good idea.
Bay Area leaders last week joined a growing chorus of local government officials across the state voicing strong opposition to Proposition 43, slamming the measure as a threat to critical financial lifelines for cities and counties.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Gov. Gavin Newsom on Friday also said he plans to vote against Prop 43, siding with a wide collection of Democratic lawmakers and local government officials who oppose the measure.
Supporters, led by the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, argue that as the state and nation grapple with an affordability crisis, raising taxes should be difficult.
General taxes, which aren’t earmarked for a specific use and go into a city’s general fund, can pass with a simple majority. But taxes that will go toward a specific purpose — like pay raises for police and fire personnel, or homeless services — are subject to a much higher two-thirds vote requirement when they’re placed on the ballot by government officials.
This puts anyone looking to raise revenue in a strange bind: Voters are much more likely to support a tax increase when they know it’s going to fix a specific problem. They’re less likely to OK a general tax hike that could fund virtually anything. Yet the two-thirds requirement is a significant hurdle, making it almost impossible to raise special taxes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 43 would extend that two-thirds threshold to special tax measures placed on the ballot by citizen initiatives, not just those spearheaded by government officials. It would mean all special taxes would need to be approved by a much higher percentage of voters than other ballot measures.
Local leaders across California, including many in the Bay Area, have begun sounding the alarm over the implications if Prop 43 were to pass.
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie, and Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee joined San Francisco Supervisor Bilal Mahmood and representatives of housing and public safety groups last week to urge voters to reject the measure, warning it would hamstring communities’ ability to raise funds for local needs. They also warned that it would enhance the veto power of a select few, potentially inviting “special interests” to try to sway election outcomes.
“Prop 43 undermines democracy by upending majority rule, making it harder for communities across California to support first responders, parks, libraries and affordable housing,” Lurie said at a press conference in San Francisco last week. “Voters know what our communities need to keep our neighborhoods safe, keep Muni moving, and build more housing.”
Supporters have cast the court decisions allowing citizens’ special tax initiatives to pass by simple majority as a loophole. If Prop 43 passes, it would essentially hit the rewind button to a period before a 2017 state Supreme Court decision led to the current simple majority rule.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association spokesperson Susan Shelley said local governments would still be able to pass general tax increases by a simple majority under Prop 43, and argued local officials should prioritize their budgets to pay for essential services first.
“Proposition 43 makes it harder to raise taxes, like sales taxes,” Shelley said. “It restores the requirement for a two-thirds vote of the people if the money from a local tax will be earmarked and locked for a special purpose.”
Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee, third from left, appears in San Francisco alongside first responders to oppose Proposition 43.
Weston Turtle Fudge/S.F. Chronicle The ballot measure also counts Reform California as a supporter, the campaign group helmed by firebrand GOP Assembly Member Carl DeMaio.
The California Republican Party, along with some Republican lawmakers and a few current and former Bay Area officials, back the measure. The list includes Debora Allen, former BART director, and Quentin Kopp, former San Francisco supervisor.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
The coalition of those fighting Prop 43 got a boost last week when Newsom endorsed a no vote, a position in lockstep with the California Democratic Party, several prominent Democratic state and local lawmakers, and associations representing California cities and counties.
The League of California Cities opposes Prop 43, as does the California State Association of Counties and the California Special Districts Association, collectively representing hundreds of municipalities across the state.
Susan Ellenberg, president of the California State Association of Counties, said in a statement to the Chronicle that many local needs depend on community-driven funding, such as wildfire prevention, emergency response and behavioral health.
“The measure would also limit residents’ ability to propose and approve solutions through the initiative process, even when those solutions earn broad majority support,” said Ellenberg, who is also a Santa Clara County supervisor. “For local governments already facing strained budgets and increasing responsibilities, this change would reshape how communities address their most pressing priorities.”
Ellenberg and other Santa Clara County leaders backed a 2024 tax increase that they billed as a measure to fund healthcare services in the wake of Trump administration cuts. But Measure A was a general tax increase, subject to the much lower vote threshold, meaning the money can technically be spent on anything. It passed with 57% of the vote.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
As of Tuesday, the Yes on 43 campaign has a slight financial edge, banking more than $10 million in campaign funds so far. The anti-43 campaign reported just under $8 million.
In 2024, eight special sales tax measures qualified for local ballots across the state by a citizens initiative, with increases ranging from one-fourth of a cent to 1 cent. Of the four that passed with a simple majority, none met Prop 43’s two-thirds vote threshold. The two that received the most support were Sonoma County’s Measure I to fund childcare and Benicia’s Measure F to fund road improvements. They passed at 62% and 61%, respectively.
Other prominent special tax measures include the Los Angeles mansion tax, which voters passed by majority in 2022 and places a 4% tax on real estate sales on multimillion-dollar homes.
Prop 43 arose out of a deal cut to avoid another qualified ballot measure from the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association that took aim at elements of the mansion tax.
It was that last-minute legislative brokering that led the anti-tax group to instead put forward Prop 43, with the help of Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland. Soon after Prop 43 qualified for the November ballot, Wicks disavowed it, calling it “the only path left to get the more dangerous initiative off the ballot.”
Isaac Martin, a sociology professor at UC San Diego who has written multiple books about taxation and public finance, described Prop 43 as affecting a Goldilocks-like subset of tax measures: popular enough for a simple majority, but not popular enough to pass overwhelmingly.
“Since it would make it harder for local governments to raise money for popular services, the options are to raise funds for general government, including popular and less popular services, or do without,” Martin said. “I mean, bottom line, those are sort of the only options for local governments.”
Groups that oppose the measure argue the new threshold would make it harder for communities to make hyper-specific funding decisions to tackle local priorities.
Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters advocacy group representing thousands of firefighters, said the measure risks cutting off crucial public safety funding. He pointed to Measure H in Sonoma County and Measure E in Los Angeles County, both passed by voters in 2024. Both taxes raise funds to bolster the two counties’ fire protection and emergency response services — top priorities in regions that have been devastated by some of the state’s deadliest wildfires in recent years.
“Any time you have local elected leaders, public safety and community advocates, or people that are running local health clinics or infrastructure projects, say that they need to get something done in their community, it should be the community that decides, with a simple majority,” Roberts said.

PROP 43: Two-Thirds Vote for Local Special Taxes
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%2043.pdf)
