California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
​​​​​​ Official ballot title: “Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.”
Type: Legislative constitutional amendment (Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22, Resolution Chapter 132, filed with the secretary of state June 25, 2026)
A vote YES means: New, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters through the initiative power would need a two-thirds vote to pass, the same threshold already required when a city council or county board places a special tax on the ballot. Local governments and their voters also could not impose ad valorem property taxes beyond the limits already in the state constitution.
A vote NO means: Certain local special taxes could continue to be approved by a simple majority vote when placed on the ballot by citizen initiative.
Sponsor/proponent: Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22 as a legislative compromise. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association drove the underlying policy and its qualified citizen initiative.
On the ballot because: The legislature placed it on the ballot by a two-thirds vote of each house on June 25, 2026, as a compromise. In exchange, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association withdrew its already-qualified initiative (AG No. 25-0006A1).
Full legal text: ACA 22, Resolution Chapter 132, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22)
LAO analysis: Legislative Analyst’s Office, Proposition 43 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 43 would raise the vote threshold for one specific path to a new local tax. Today, when a city council or county board of supervisors asks voters to approve a special tax, meaning a tax earmarked for a specific purpose, that tax needs a two-thirds vote to pass. That requirement traces to Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996. A separate path exists. When voters themselves place a special tax on the ballot through the citizen initiative, a series of court decisions has allowed that tax to pass with a simple majority. Proposition 43 would close that gap. Beginning January 1, 2027, a voter-initiated local special tax would need the same two-thirds vote as a government-sponsored one.
The measure carries a second provision that has drawn less attention. It also bars a local government, including its electorate acting by initiative, from imposing ad valorem taxes on real property beyond the 1 percent rate that Proposition 13 already allows. This extends the existing constitutional limit so that it cannot be worked around through the initiative power.
The Legislative Analyst’s Office frames the practical effect plainly. By raising the bar for these taxes, the measure makes it harder for local governments to raise certain revenues, so local tax collections could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The office adds that the actual impact is unknown and would depend on future choices by voters and local officials.
2. The legal language
Full text: ACA 22, “Local Taxes: Limitation,” Resolution Chapter 132, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22) (filed with the secretary of state June 25, 2026)
Key language:
“Beginning on January 1, 2027, and notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax, except as provided in Section 4 of this article, subdivision (d) of Section 2 of Article XIII C, and paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D, unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote.” [1, Sec. 4.5(a)]
What it amends: Adds Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution, the article created by Proposition 13. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal it on its own. The phrase “including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power” is the operative change, since it applies the two-thirds requirement to citizen initiatives, which recent court rulings had exempted.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22, but she did so as the vehicle for a negotiated deal rather than as a personal cause, and she has since said she opposes the measure. The policy behind it belongs to the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and its president, Jon Coupal, who had qualified a broader citizen initiative and agreed to pull it once the legislature placed this narrower version on the ballot. Opposition comes from transit, housing, and local government advocates who rely on majority-vote initiatives to fund services.
What? A two-thirds vote requirement for voter-initiated local special taxes, plus a bar on using the initiative power to impose ad valorem property taxes beyond the existing 1 percent limit.
Where? Statewide in effect, but it governs local taxes, so its bite is felt in the cities, counties, and special districts where citizen tax initiatives appear.
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. The requirement applies to taxes beginning January 1, 2027.
Why? Supporters argue that a special tax is a special tax no matter who puts it on the ballot, and that letting initiatives pass earmarked taxes by a simple majority is an end run around a taxpayer protection that has stood since Proposition 13. Opponents argue that the citizen initiative is a core democratic tool and that a supermajority requirement lets a minority of voters block services the majority wants.
4. Trade-offs
For roughly two decades after Proposition 218, most people assumed every local special tax needed two-thirds approval. The California Supreme Court unsettled that assumption in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017), holding that the procedural limits Proposition 218 placed on local governments do not automatically bind voters acting through the initiative. The court itself called the change modest and left the two-thirds question open. Lower courts then took the next step, upholding several citizen special taxes that had passed with a majority rather than a two-thirds vote. That line of cases is what Proposition 43 would overturn.
The trade-off is real on both sides. The measure closes what supporters see as a loophole that lets organized campaigns pass targeted taxes with less consensus than the state constitution otherwise demands. A two-thirds rule protects the minority who bear the tax, and it forces broad agreement before money is committed to a single purpose. But the same rule is a powerful brake. Supermajority requirements let roughly one-third of voters defeat what a majority supports, and the taxes that have passed by majority under the current rule are not abstractions. They have funded things like fire protection, health services, and open-space preservation in specific counties. Under Proposition 43 several of those recent measures would have failed despite winning majority support.
There is also a worthwhile point about scope. Proposition 43 is deliberately narrower than the initiative it replaced. The original Howard Jarvis measure would also have restricted certain charter-city real estate transfer taxes and would have reached backward to invalidate some taxes already in place. ACA 22 drops both of those features and applies only going forward. Voters weighing this measure are voting on the prospective threshold change and the ad valorem limit, not on the more sweeping version that was withdrawn.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
It restores a single, consistent rule. A local special tax would need two-thirds approval regardless of whether a city council or a citizen initiative places it on the ballot, ending a distinction that turned on procedure rather than substance.
It strengthens a long-standing taxpayer protection. The two-thirds requirement for earmarked local taxes has been part of California law since Proposition 13 and Proposition 218, and the measure keeps the initiative power from bypassing it.
It is prospective and narrow. Unlike the withdrawn initiative, it does not invalidate existing taxes or add new limits on real estate transfer taxes, which reduces the risk of disruptively unwinding revenue already budgeted.
It adds certainty. Litigation since Upland left the majority-versus-two-thirds question unsettled for years, and a clear constitutional rule would end that ambiguity.
Potential risks
It makes it harder to fund local services. The Legislative Analyst finds local tax revenues could be lower than they otherwise would be, though the size of the effect is unknown.
It lets a minority block a majority. A tax with 60 percent support would fail, so about one-third of voters could defeat a measure the majority favors.
It narrows a core democratic tool. The citizen initiative was designed to let voters act when their elected officials will not, and the measure raises the bar specifically for that path.
Real recent examples would have failed. Several county special taxes for fire, health, and open space passed with majorities below two-thirds and would not have survived this rule.
The ad valorem provision is easy to overlook. Most coverage focuses on the vote threshold, yet the measure also writes a real property tax limit into the constitution, and its practical reach deserves scrutiny.
6. Open questions
How many recent local special taxes actually passed with between a majority and two-thirds vote, and how much revenue statewide would have been at stake under the new rule?
Does the ad valorem provision in subdivision (b) change anything on the ground, or does it mainly codify limits that courts already enforced?
Will the narrower ACA 22 satisfy the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association over time, or does the withdrawn initiative signal a broader effort to come?
How will the measure interact with the exceptions it cross-references in Article XIII C and Article XIII D, and which taxes fall inside or outside those carve-outs?
With the author now opposed to her own measure, how will the yes and no campaigns be organized and funded?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
A special tax funds one specific thing, and the state constitution has long asked for two-thirds approval before a city or county can levy one. Should the same two-thirds rule apply when voters put that tax on the ballot themselves, or should the citizen initiative be a path to a simple-majority tax that elected officials could not pass on their own?
Ask which risk worries you more: A supermajority rule that lets one-third of voters block services the majority wants, or a majority rule that lets an organized campaign commit a community to a targeted tax with less consensus than the constitution otherwise requires?

Quick Facts
​​​​​​ Official ballot title: “Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.”
Type: Legislative constitutional amendment (Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22, Resolution Chapter 132, filed with the secretary of state June 25, 2026)
A vote YES means: New, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters through the initiative power would need a two-thirds vote to pass, the same threshold already required when a city council or county board places a special tax on the ballot. Local governments and their voters also could not impose ad valorem property taxes beyond the limits already in the state constitution.
A vote NO means: Certain local special taxes could continue to be approved by a simple majority vote when placed on the ballot by citizen initiative.
Sponsor/proponent: Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22 as a legislative compromise. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association drove the underlying policy and its qualified citizen initiative.
On the ballot because: The legislature placed it on the ballot by a two-thirds vote of each house on June 25, 2026, as a compromise. In exchange, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association withdrew its already-qualified initiative (AG No. 25-0006A1).
Full legal text: ACA 22, Resolution Chapter 132, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22)
LAO analysis: Legislative Analyst’s Office, Proposition 43 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 43 would raise the vote threshold for one specific path to a new local tax. Today, when a city council or county board of supervisors asks voters to approve a special tax, meaning a tax earmarked for a specific purpose, that tax needs a two-thirds vote to pass. That requirement traces to Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996. A separate path exists. When voters themselves place a special tax on the ballot through the citizen initiative, a series of court decisions has allowed that tax to pass with a simple majority. Proposition 43 would close that gap. Beginning January 1, 2027, a voter-initiated local special tax would need the same two-thirds vote as a government-sponsored one.
The measure carries a second provision that has drawn less attention. It also bars a local government, including its electorate acting by initiative, from imposing ad valorem taxes on real property beyond the 1 percent rate that Proposition 13 already allows. This extends the existing constitutional limit so that it cannot be worked around through the initiative power.
The Legislative Analyst’s Office frames the practical effect plainly. By raising the bar for these taxes, the measure makes it harder for local governments to raise certain revenues, so local tax collections could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The office adds that the actual impact is unknown and would depend on future choices by voters and local officials.
2. The legal language
Full text: ACA 22, “Local Taxes: Limitation,” Resolution Chapter 132, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22) (filed with the secretary of state June 25, 2026)
Key language:
“Beginning on January 1, 2027, and notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax, except as provided in Section 4 of this article, subdivision (d) of Section 2 of Article XIII C, and paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D, unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote.” [1, Sec. 4.5(a)]
What it amends: Adds Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution, the article created by Proposition 13. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal it on its own. The phrase “including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power” is the operative change, since it applies the two-thirds requirement to citizen initiatives, which recent court rulings had exempted.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22, but she did so as the vehicle for a negotiated deal rather than as a personal cause, and she has since said she opposes the measure. The policy behind it belongs to the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and its president, Jon Coupal, who had qualified a broader citizen initiative and agreed to pull it once the legislature placed this narrower version on the ballot. Opposition comes from transit, housing, and local government advocates who rely on majority-vote initiatives to fund services.
What? A two-thirds vote requirement for voter-initiated local special taxes, plus a bar on using the initiative power to impose ad valorem property taxes beyond the existing 1 percent limit.
Where? Statewide in effect, but it governs local taxes, so its bite is felt in the cities, counties, and special districts where citizen tax initiatives appear.
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. The requirement applies to taxes beginning January 1, 2027.
Why? Supporters argue that a special tax is a special tax no matter who puts it on the ballot, and that letting initiatives pass earmarked taxes by a simple majority is an end run around a taxpayer protection that has stood since Proposition 13. Opponents argue that the citizen initiative is a core democratic tool and that a supermajority requirement lets a minority of voters block services the majority wants.
4. Trade-offs
For roughly two decades after Proposition 218, most people assumed every local special tax needed two-thirds approval. The California Supreme Court unsettled that assumption in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017), holding that the procedural limits Proposition 218 placed on local governments do not automatically bind voters acting through the initiative. The court itself called the change modest and left the two-thirds question open. Lower courts then took the next step, upholding several citizen special taxes that had passed with a majority rather than a two-thirds vote. That line of cases is what Proposition 43 would overturn.
The trade-off is real on both sides. The measure closes what supporters see as a loophole that lets organized campaigns pass targeted taxes with less consensus than the state constitution otherwise demands. A two-thirds rule protects the minority who bear the tax, and it forces broad agreement before money is committed to a single purpose. But the same rule is a powerful brake. Supermajority requirements let roughly one-third of voters defeat what a majority supports, and the taxes that have passed by majority under the current rule are not abstractions. They have funded things like fire protection, health services, and open-space preservation in specific counties. Under Proposition 43 several of those recent measures would have failed despite winning majority support.
There is also a worthwhile point about scope. Proposition 43 is deliberately narrower than the initiative it replaced. The original Howard Jarvis measure would also have restricted certain charter-city real estate transfer taxes and would have reached backward to invalidate some taxes already in place. ACA 22 drops both of those features and applies only going forward. Voters weighing this measure are voting on the prospective threshold change and the ad valorem limit, not on the more sweeping version that was withdrawn.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
It restores a single, consistent rule. A local special tax would need two-thirds approval regardless of whether a city council or a citizen initiative places it on the ballot, ending a distinction that turned on procedure rather than substance.
It strengthens a long-standing taxpayer protection. The two-thirds requirement for earmarked local taxes has been part of California law since Proposition 13 and Proposition 218, and the measure keeps the initiative power from bypassing it.
It is prospective and narrow. Unlike the withdrawn initiative, it does not invalidate existing taxes or add new limits on real estate transfer taxes, which reduces the risk of disruptively unwinding revenue already budgeted.
It adds certainty. Litigation since Upland left the majority-versus-two-thirds question unsettled for years, and a clear constitutional rule would end that ambiguity.
Potential risks
It makes it harder to fund local services. The Legislative Analyst finds local tax revenues could be lower than they otherwise would be, though the size of the effect is unknown.
It lets a minority block a majority. A tax with 60 percent support would fail, so about one-third of voters could defeat a measure the majority favors.
It narrows a core democratic tool. The citizen initiative was designed to let voters act when their elected officials will not, and the measure raises the bar specifically for that path.
Real recent examples would have failed. Several county special taxes for fire, health, and open space passed with majorities below two-thirds and would not have survived this rule.
The ad valorem provision is easy to overlook. Most coverage focuses on the vote threshold, yet the measure also writes a real property tax limit into the constitution, and its practical reach deserves scrutiny.
6. Open questions
How many recent local special taxes actually passed with between a majority and two-thirds vote, and how much revenue statewide would have been at stake under the new rule?
Does the ad valorem provision in subdivision (b) change anything on the ground, or does it mainly codify limits that courts already enforced?
Will the narrower ACA 22 satisfy the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association over time, or does the withdrawn initiative signal a broader effort to come?
How will the measure interact with the exceptions it cross-references in Article XIII C and Article XIII D, and which taxes fall inside or outside those carve-outs?
With the author now opposed to her own measure, how will the yes and no campaigns be organized and funded?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
A special tax funds one specific thing, and the state constitution has long asked for two-thirds approval before a city or county can levy one. Should the same two-thirds rule apply when voters put that tax on the ballot themselves, or should the citizen initiative be a path to a simple-majority tax that elected officials could not pass on their own?

Requires a Two-Thirds Vote to Approve Local Special Tax Initiatives
PROP
43 Purpose
Proposition 43 is a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature that would raise the
vote share required to enact special tax initiatives proposed by citizens from a simple majority
to a two-thirds majority.1
CALIFORNIA
Research Assistant: Kahani Malhotra ’27
Background
In 1978, California voters passed Proposition 13, requiring that any special tax proposed by a
local government must receive a two-thirds vote from the electorate before being enacted,2
with a special tax being defined as any tax imposed for a specific purpose rather than general
governmental need.3 In 1996, Proposition 218 further increased the power of voters to approve
taxes by requiring that any general tax imposed by a local government must receive majority
voter approval, and reaffirmed that special taxes require two-thirds voter approval.4
Two decades later, a court decision narrowed the scope of Proposition 218. In 2017, the
California Supreme Court ruled in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland that a significant
requirement for general taxes — that they be placed on the ballot during general elections —
did not apply to citizen initiatives.5 Ultimately, the court categorized taxes imposed by local
governments as different from taxes imposed by citizen initiatives.
The ruling raised an important question: Are special taxes imposed by citizen initiatives exempt
from the two-thirds vote requirement that applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local
governments? A memo from the San Francisco attorney’s office interpreting the ruling seemed
to indicate that the answer was yes.6 But the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association disagreed.
In 2018, the Association sued San Francisco for allowing two separate citizen-driven measures
to pass with a simple-majority vote rather than a supermajority vote. A judge ruled against the
Association, affirming that the special tax measures were rightfully passed by majority vote
since they were proposed by citizens.7 A state appeals court shot down the Association’s further
attempts to overturn citizen-initiated local taxes passed in 20208 and 2021.9
In 2023, the Association and the California Business Roundtable qualified an initiative10 for the
2024 ballot cycle that would have mandated any special tax initiative to require a two-thirds
majority vote regardless of whether a local government or citizens proposed it.11 But in June
2024, the California Supreme Court ruled unanimously that passage of the initiative would lead
to a “revision,” rather than an amendment, of the state constitution, “based on its far-reaching
changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained at the
state and local levels.” While amendments may be made by citizen initiatives, revisions require
“a constitutional convention and popular ratification.”12 Thus, enacting the proposal by initiative
would be unconstitutional.
In 2026, the same two organizations qualified an initiative for the 2026 general election
ballot that would have amended the state constitution to require a two-thirds majority to pass
citizen-led local special tax initiatives, alongside other tax limiting provisions.13 Following a
legislative compromise, which included the passage of ACA 22,14 the organizations withdrew the
initiative in favor of Proposition 43 being placed on this year’s ballot as a legislatively referred
constitutional amendment.15 Though ACA 22 passed nearly unanimously in the Assembly (68-2)
and Senate (35-1), its author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-14), announced on June 29 that
she was “adamantly opposed to it.16
Proposal
Proposition 43 would amend the
California Constitution to require that
citizen-driven special tax initiatives
require a two-thirds majority vote
for passage. It would add Section
4.5 to Article XIII A of the California
Constitution, detailing that any local
government — including voters
within a local government exercising
the initiative power — must obtain
a two-thirds vote to enact, extend,
or increase a special tax starting on
January 1, 2027.
The amendment also prohibits local
government and members of the
electorate from levying ad valorem
property taxes — taxes based on the
value of real estate or tangible per-
sonal property — except for certain
preapproved, dedicated property
taxes, whose terms are delineated in
the Constitution.17
Fiscal Impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s
Office (LAO) estimates that Propo-
sition 43 would reduce local govern-
ment tax revenues. The total fiscal
impact is largely unknown, however,
as it depends on future decisions by
voters and local governments.18

Requires a Two-Thirds Vote to Approve Local Special Tax Initiatives
PROP
43 Purpose
Proposition 43 is a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature that would raise the
vote share required to enact special tax initiatives proposed by citizens from a simple majority
to a two-thirds majority.1
CALIFORNIA
Research Assistant: Kahani Malhotra ’27
Background
In 1978, California voters passed Proposition 13, requiring that any special tax proposed by a
local government must receive a two-thirds vote from the electorate before being enacted,2
with a special tax being defined as any tax imposed for a specific purpose rather than general
governmental need.3 In 1996, Proposition 218 further increased the power of voters to approve
taxes by requiring that any general tax imposed by a local government must receive majority
voter approval, and reaffirmed that special taxes require two-thirds voter approval.4
Two decades later, a court decision narrowed the scope of Proposition 218. In 2017, the
California Supreme Court ruled in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland that a significant
requirement for general taxes — that they be placed on the ballot during general elections —
did not apply to citizen initiatives.5 Ultimately, the court categorized taxes imposed by local
governments as different from taxes imposed by citizen initiatives.
The ruling raised an important question: Are special taxes imposed by citizen initiatives exempt
from the two-thirds vote requirement that applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local
governments? A memo from the San Francisco attorney’s office interpreting the ruling seemed
to indicate that the answer was yes.6 But the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association disagreed.
In 2018, the Association sued San Francisco for allowing two separate citizen-driven measures
to pass with a simple-majority vote rather than a supermajority vote. A judge ruled against the
Association, affirming that the special tax measures were rightfully passed by majority vote
since they were proposed by citizens.7 A state appeals court shot down the Association’s further
attempts to overturn citizen-initiated local taxes passed in 20208 and 2021.9
In 2023, the Association and the California Business Roundtable qualified an initiative10 for the
2024 ballot cycle that would have mandated any special tax initiative to require a two-thirds
majority vote regardless of whether a local government or citizens proposed it.11 But in June
2024, the California Supreme Court ruled unanimously that passage of the initiative would lead
to a “revision,” rather than an amendment, of the state constitution, “based on its far-reaching
changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained at the
state and local levels.” While amendments may be made by citizen initiatives, revisions require
“a constitutional convention and popular ratification.”12 Thus, enacting the proposal by initiative
would be unconstitutional.
In 2026, the same two organizations qualified an initiative for the 2026 general election
ballot that would have amended the state constitution to require a two-thirds majority to pass
citizen-led local special tax initiatives, alongside other tax limiting provisions.13 Following a
legislative compromise, which included the passage of ACA 22,14 the organizations withdrew the
initiative in favor of Proposition 43 being placed on this year’s ballot as a legislatively referred
constitutional amendment.15 Though ACA 22 passed nearly unanimously in the Assembly (68-2)
and Senate (35-1), its author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-14), announced on June 29 that
she was “adamantly opposed to it.16
Proposal
Proposition 43 would amend the
California Constitution to require that
citizen-driven special tax initiatives
require a two-thirds majority vote
for passage. It would add Section
4.5 to Article XIII A of the California
Constitution, detailing that any local
government — including voters
within a local government exercising
the initiative power — must obtain
a two-thirds vote to enact, extend,
or increase a special tax starting on
January 1, 2027.
The amendment also prohibits local
government and members of the
electorate from levying ad valorem
property taxes — taxes based on the
value of real estate or tangible per-
sonal property — except for certain
preapproved, dedicated property
taxes, whose terms are delineated in
the Constitution.17
Fiscal Impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s
Office (LAO) estimates that Propo-
sition 43 would reduce local govern-
ment tax revenues. The total fiscal
impact is largely unknown, however,
as it depends on future decisions by
voters and local governments.18

Bay Area officials are sounding the alarm over a lesser-known California ballot measure
By Kathryn Palmer (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/kathryn-palmer/) , Staff Writer Oct 12, 2026
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie appears alongside first responders to oppose Proposition 43 outside of Fire Station No. 5 on Oct. 7.
Weston Turtle Fudge/S.F. Chronicle
It’s not often that the supporters and opponents of a ballot measure agree on what exactly it would do, let alone describe it the same way. Yet both sides of the fight over Proposition 43 have been clear: It will make it harder to raise local taxes.
What they don’t agree on is whether it’s a good idea.
Bay Area leaders last week joined a growing chorus of local government officials across the state voicing strong opposition to Proposition 43, slamming the measure as a threat to critical financial lifelines for cities and counties.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Gov. Gavin Newsom on Friday also said he plans to vote against Prop 43, siding with a wide collection of Democratic lawmakers and local government officials who oppose the measure.
Supporters, led by the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, argue that as the state and nation grapple with an affordability crisis, raising taxes should be difficult.
General taxes, which aren’t earmarked for a specific use and go into a city’s general fund, can pass with a simple majority. But taxes that will go toward a specific purpose — like pay raises for police and fire personnel, or homeless services — are subject to a much higher two-thirds vote requirement when they’re placed on the ballot by government officials.
This puts anyone looking to raise revenue in a strange bind: Voters are much more likely to support a tax increase when they know it’s going to fix a specific problem. They’re less likely to OK a general tax hike that could fund virtually anything. Yet the two-thirds requirement is a significant hurdle, making it almost impossible to raise special taxes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 43 would extend that two-thirds threshold to special tax measures placed on the ballot by citizen initiatives, not just those spearheaded by government officials. It would mean all special taxes would need to be approved by a much higher percentage of voters than other ballot measures.
Local leaders across California, including many in the Bay Area, have begun sounding the alarm over the implications if Prop 43 were to pass.
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie, and Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee joined San Francisco Supervisor Bilal Mahmood and representatives of housing and public safety groups last week to urge voters to reject the measure, warning it would hamstring communities’ ability to raise funds for local needs. They also warned that it would enhance the veto power of a select few, potentially inviting “special interests” to try to sway election outcomes.
“Prop 43 undermines democracy by upending majority rule, making it harder for communities across California to support first responders, parks, libraries and affordable housing,” Lurie said at a press conference in San Francisco last week. “Voters know what our communities need to keep our neighborhoods safe, keep Muni moving, and build more housing.”
Supporters have cast the court decisions allowing citizens’ special tax initiatives to pass by simple majority as a loophole. If Prop 43 passes, it would essentially hit the rewind button to a period before a 2017 state Supreme Court decision led to the current simple majority rule.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association spokesperson Susan Shelley said local governments would still be able to pass general tax increases by a simple majority under Prop 43, and argued local officials should prioritize their budgets to pay for essential services first.
“Proposition 43 makes it harder to raise taxes, like sales taxes,” Shelley said. “It restores the requirement for a two-thirds vote of the people if the money from a local tax will be earmarked and locked for a special purpose.”
Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee, third from left, appears in San Francisco alongside first responders to oppose Proposition 43.
Weston Turtle Fudge/S.F. Chronicle The ballot measure also counts Reform California as a supporter, the campaign group helmed by firebrand GOP Assembly Member Carl DeMaio.
The California Republican Party, along with some Republican lawmakers and a few current and former Bay Area officials, back the measure. The list includes Debora Allen, former BART director, and Quentin Kopp, former San Francisco supervisor.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
The coalition of those fighting Prop 43 got a boost last week when Newsom endorsed a no vote, a position in lockstep with the California Democratic Party, several prominent Democratic state and local lawmakers, and associations representing California cities and counties.
The League of California Cities opposes Prop 43, as does the California State Association of Counties and the California Special Districts Association, collectively representing hundreds of municipalities across the state.
Susan Ellenberg, president of the California State Association of Counties, said in a statement to the Chronicle that many local needs depend on community-driven funding, such as wildfire prevention, emergency response and behavioral health.
“The measure would also limit residents’ ability to propose and approve solutions through the initiative process, even when those solutions earn broad majority support,” said Ellenberg, who is also a Santa Clara County supervisor. “For local governments already facing strained budgets and increasing responsibilities, this change would reshape how communities address their most pressing priorities.”
Ellenberg and other Santa Clara County leaders backed a 2024 tax increase that they billed as a measure to fund healthcare services in the wake of Trump administration cuts. But Measure A was a general tax increase, subject to the much lower vote threshold, meaning the money can technically be spent on anything. It passed with 57% of the vote.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
As of Tuesday, the Yes on 43 campaign has a slight financial edge, banking more than $10 million in campaign funds so far. The anti-43 campaign reported just under $8 million.
In 2024, eight special sales tax measures qualified for local ballots across the state by a citizens initiative, with increases ranging from one-fourth of a cent to 1 cent. Of the four that passed with a simple majority, none met Prop 43’s two-thirds vote threshold. The two that received the most support were Sonoma County’s Measure I to fund childcare and Benicia’s Measure F to fund road improvements. They passed at 62% and 61%, respectively.
Other prominent special tax measures include the Los Angeles mansion tax, which voters passed by majority in 2022 and places a 4% tax on real estate sales on multimillion-dollar homes.
Prop 43 arose out of a deal cut to avoid another qualified ballot measure from the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association that took aim at elements of the mansion tax.
It was that last-minute legislative brokering that led the anti-tax group to instead put forward Prop 43, with the help of Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland. Soon after Prop 43 qualified for the November ballot, Wicks disavowed it, calling it “the only path left to get the more dangerous initiative off the ballot.”
Isaac Martin, a sociology professor at UC San Diego who has written multiple books about taxation and public finance, described Prop 43 as affecting a Goldilocks-like subset of tax measures: popular enough for a simple majority, but not popular enough to pass overwhelmingly.
“Since it would make it harder for local governments to raise money for popular services, the options are to raise funds for general government, including popular and less popular services, or do without,” Martin said. “I mean, bottom line, those are sort of the only options for local governments.”
Groups that oppose the measure argue the new threshold would make it harder for communities to make hyper-specific funding decisions to tackle local priorities.
Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters advocacy group representing thousands of firefighters, said the measure risks cutting off crucial public safety funding. He pointed to Measure H in Sonoma County and Measure E in Los Angeles County, both passed by voters in 2024. Both taxes raise funds to bolster the two counties’ fire protection and emergency response services — top priorities in regions that have been devastated by some of the state’s deadliest wildfires in recent years.
“Any time you have local elected leaders, public safety and community advocates, or people that are running local health clinics or infrastructure projects, say that they need to get something done in their community, it should be the community that decides, with a simple majority,” Roberts said.

Bay Area officials are sounding the alarm over a lesser-known California ballot measure
By Kathryn Palmer (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/kathryn-palmer/) , Staff Writer Oct 12, 2026
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie appears alongside first responders to oppose Proposition 43 outside of Fire Station No. 5 on Oct. 7.
Weston Turtle Fudge/S.F. Chronicle
It’s not often that the supporters and opponents of a ballot measure agree on what exactly it would do, let alone describe it the same way. Yet both sides of the fight over Proposition 43 have been clear: It will make it harder to raise local taxes.
What they don’t agree on is whether it’s a good idea.
Bay Area leaders last week joined a growing chorus of local government officials across the state voicing strong opposition to Proposition 43, slamming the measure as a threat to critical financial lifelines for cities and counties.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Gov. Gavin Newsom on Friday also said he plans to vote against Prop 43, siding with a wide collection of Democratic lawmakers and local government officials who oppose the measure.
Supporters, led by the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, argue that as the state and nation grapple with an affordability crisis, raising taxes should be difficult.
General taxes, which aren’t earmarked for a specific use and go into a city’s general fund, can pass with a simple majority. But taxes that will go toward a specific purpose — like pay raises for police and fire personnel, or homeless services — are subject to a much higher two-thirds vote requirement when they’re placed on the ballot by government officials.
This puts anyone looking to raise revenue in a strange bind: Voters are much more likely to support a tax increase when they know it’s going to fix a specific problem. They’re less likely to OK a general tax hike that could fund virtually anything. Yet the two-thirds requirement is a significant hurdle, making it almost impossible to raise special taxes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 43 would extend that two-thirds threshold to special tax measures placed on the ballot by citizen initiatives, not just those spearheaded by government officials. It would mean all special taxes would need to be approved by a much higher percentage of voters than other ballot measures.
Local leaders across California, including many in the Bay Area, have begun sounding the alarm over the implications if Prop 43 were to pass.
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie, and Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee joined San Francisco Supervisor Bilal Mahmood and representatives of housing and public safety groups last week to urge voters to reject the measure, warning it would hamstring communities’ ability to raise funds for local needs. They also warned that it would enhance the veto power of a select few, potentially inviting “special interests” to try to sway election outcomes.
“Prop 43 undermines democracy by upending majority rule, making it harder for communities across California to support first responders, parks, libraries and affordable housing,” Lurie said at a press conference in San Francisco last week. “Voters know what our communities need to keep our neighborhoods safe, keep Muni moving, and build more housing.”
Supporters have cast the court decisions allowing citizens’ special tax initiatives to pass by simple majority as a loophole. If Prop 43 passes, it would essentially hit the rewind button to a period before a 2017 state Supreme Court decision led to the current simple majority rule.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association spokesperson Susan Shelley said local governments would still be able to pass general tax increases by a simple majority under Prop 43, and argued local officials should prioritize their budgets to pay for essential services first.
“Proposition 43 makes it harder to raise taxes, like sales taxes,” Shelley said. “It restores the requirement for a two-thirds vote of the people if the money from a local tax will be earmarked and locked for a special purpose.”
Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee, third from left, appears in San Francisco alongside first responders to oppose Proposition 43.
Weston Turtle Fudge/S.F. Chronicle The ballot measure also counts Reform California as a supporter, the campaign group helmed by firebrand GOP Assembly Member Carl DeMaio.
The California Republican Party, along with some Republican lawmakers and a few current and former Bay Area officials, back the measure. The list includes Debora Allen, former BART director, and Quentin Kopp, former San Francisco supervisor.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
The coalition of those fighting Prop 43 got a boost last week when Newsom endorsed a no vote, a position in lockstep with the California Democratic Party, several prominent Democratic state and local lawmakers, and associations representing California cities and counties.
The League of California Cities opposes Prop 43, as does the California State Association of Counties and the California Special Districts Association, collectively representing hundreds of municipalities across the state.
Susan Ellenberg, president of the California State Association of Counties, said in a statement to the Chronicle that many local needs depend on community-driven funding, such as wildfire prevention, emergency response and behavioral health.
“The measure would also limit residents’ ability to propose and approve solutions through the initiative process, even when those solutions earn broad majority support,” said Ellenberg, who is also a Santa Clara County supervisor. “For local governments already facing strained budgets and increasing responsibilities, this change would reshape how communities address their most pressing priorities.”
Ellenberg and other Santa Clara County leaders backed a 2024 tax increase that they billed as a measure to fund healthcare services in the wake of Trump administration cuts. But Measure A was a general tax increase, subject to the much lower vote threshold, meaning the money can technically be spent on anything. It passed with 57% of the vote.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
As of Tuesday, the Yes on 43 campaign has a slight financial edge, banking more than $10 million in campaign funds so far. The anti-43 campaign reported just under $8 million.
In 2024, eight special sales tax measures qualified for local ballots across the state by a citizens initiative, with increases ranging from one-fourth of a cent to 1 cent. Of the four that passed with a simple majority, none met Prop 43’s two-thirds vote threshold. The two that received the most support were Sonoma County’s Measure I to fund childcare and Benicia’s Measure F to fund road improvements. They passed at 62% and 61%, respectively.
Other prominent special tax measures include the Los Angeles mansion tax, which voters passed by majority in 2022 and places a 4% tax on real estate sales on multimillion-dollar homes.
Prop 43 arose out of a deal cut to avoid another qualified ballot measure from the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association that took aim at elements of the mansion tax.
It was that last-minute legislative brokering that led the anti-tax group to instead put forward Prop 43, with the help of Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland. Soon after Prop 43 qualified for the November ballot, Wicks disavowed it, calling it “the only path left to get the more dangerous initiative off the ballot.”
Isaac Martin, a sociology professor at UC San Diego who has written multiple books about taxation and public finance, described Prop 43 as affecting a Goldilocks-like subset of tax measures: popular enough for a simple majority, but not popular enough to pass overwhelmingly.
“Since it would make it harder for local governments to raise money for popular services, the options are to raise funds for general government, including popular and less popular services, or do without,” Martin said. “I mean, bottom line, those are sort of the only options for local governments.”
Groups that oppose the measure argue the new threshold would make it harder for communities to make hyper-specific funding decisions to tackle local priorities.
Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters advocacy group representing thousands of firefighters, said the measure risks cutting off crucial public safety funding. He pointed to Measure H in Sonoma County and Measure E in Los Angeles County, both passed by voters in 2024. Both taxes raise funds to bolster the two counties’ fire protection and emergency response services — top priorities in regions that have been devastated by some of the state’s deadliest wildfires in recent years.
“Any time you have local elected leaders, public safety and community advocates, or people that are running local health clinics or infrastructure projects, say that they need to get something done in their community, it should be the community that decides, with a simple majority,” Roberts said.

Quick Facts
​​​​​​ Official ballot title: “Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.”
Type: Legislative constitutional amendment (Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22, Resolution Chapter 132, filed with the secretary of state June 25, 2026)
A vote YES means: New, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters through the initiative power would need a two-thirds vote to pass, the same threshold already required when a city council or county board places a special tax on the ballot. Local governments and their voters also could not impose ad valorem property taxes beyond the limits already in the state constitution.
A vote NO means: Certain local special taxes could continue to be approved by a simple majority vote when placed on the ballot by citizen initiative.
Sponsor/proponent: Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22 as a legislative compromise. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association drove the underlying policy and its qualified citizen initiative.
On the ballot because: The legislature placed it on the ballot by a two-thirds vote of each house on June 25, 2026, as a compromise. In exchange, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association withdrew its already-qualified initiative (AG No. 25-0006A1).
Full legal text: ACA 22, Resolution Chapter 132, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22)
LAO analysis: Legislative Analyst’s Office, Proposition 43 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 43 would raise the vote threshold for one specific path to a new local tax. Today, when a city council or county board of supervisors asks voters to approve a special tax, meaning a tax earmarked for a specific purpose, that tax needs a two-thirds vote to pass. That requirement traces to Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996. A separate path exists. When voters themselves place a special tax on the ballot through the citizen initiative, a series of court decisions has allowed that tax to pass with a simple majority. Proposition 43 would close that gap. Beginning January 1, 2027, a voter-initiated local special tax would need the same two-thirds vote as a government-sponsored one.
The measure carries a second provision that has drawn less attention. It also bars a local government, including its electorate acting by initiative, from imposing ad valorem taxes on real property beyond the 1 percent rate that Proposition 13 already allows. This extends the existing constitutional limit so that it cannot be worked around through the initiative power.
The Legislative Analyst’s Office frames the practical effect plainly. By raising the bar for these taxes, the measure makes it harder for local governments to raise certain revenues, so local tax collections could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The office adds that the actual impact is unknown and would depend on future choices by voters and local officials.
2. The legal language
Full text: ACA 22, “Local Taxes: Limitation,” Resolution Chapter 132, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22) (filed with the secretary of state June 25, 2026)
Key language:
“Beginning on January 1, 2027, and notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax, except as provided in Section 4 of this article, subdivision (d) of Section 2 of Article XIII C, and paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D, unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote.” [1, Sec. 4.5(a)]
What it amends: Adds Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution, the article created by Proposition 13. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal it on its own. The phrase “including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power” is the operative change, since it applies the two-thirds requirement to citizen initiatives, which recent court rulings had exempted.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22, but she did so as the vehicle for a negotiated deal rather than as a personal cause, and she has since said she opposes the measure. The policy behind it belongs to the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and its president, Jon Coupal, who had qualified a broader citizen initiative and agreed to pull it once the legislature placed this narrower version on the ballot. Opposition comes from transit, housing, and local government advocates who rely on majority-vote initiatives to fund services.
What? A two-thirds vote requirement for voter-initiated local special taxes, plus a bar on using the initiative power to impose ad valorem property taxes beyond the existing 1 percent limit.
Where? Statewide in effect, but it governs local taxes, so its bite is felt in the cities, counties, and special districts where citizen tax initiatives appear.
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. The requirement applies to taxes beginning January 1, 2027.
Why? Supporters argue that a special tax is a special tax no matter who puts it on the ballot, and that letting initiatives pass earmarked taxes by a simple majority is an end run around a taxpayer protection that has stood since Proposition 13. Opponents argue that the citizen initiative is a core democratic tool and that a supermajority requirement lets a minority of voters block services the majority wants.
4. Trade-offs
For roughly two decades after Proposition 218, most people assumed every local special tax needed two-thirds approval. The California Supreme Court unsettled that assumption in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017), holding that the procedural limits Proposition 218 placed on local governments do not automatically bind voters acting through the initiative. The court itself called the change modest and left the two-thirds question open. Lower courts then took the next step, upholding several citizen special taxes that had passed with a majority rather than a two-thirds vote. That line of cases is what Proposition 43 would overturn.
The trade-off is real on both sides. The measure closes what supporters see as a loophole that lets organized campaigns pass targeted taxes with less consensus than the state constitution otherwise demands. A two-thirds rule protects the minority who bear the tax, and it forces broad agreement before money is committed to a single purpose. But the same rule is a powerful brake. Supermajority requirements let roughly one-third of voters defeat what a majority supports, and the taxes that have passed by majority under the current rule are not abstractions. They have funded things like fire protection, health services, and open-space preservation in specific counties. Under Proposition 43 several of those recent measures would have failed despite winning majority support.
There is also a worthwhile point about scope. Proposition 43 is deliberately narrower than the initiative it replaced. The original Howard Jarvis measure would also have restricted certain charter-city real estate transfer taxes and would have reached backward to invalidate some taxes already in place. ACA 22 drops both of those features and applies only going forward. Voters weighing this measure are voting on the prospective threshold change and the ad valorem limit, not on the more sweeping version that was withdrawn.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
It restores a single, consistent rule. A local special tax would need two-thirds approval regardless of whether a city council or a citizen initiative places it on the ballot, ending a distinction that turned on procedure rather than substance.
It strengthens a long-standing taxpayer protection. The two-thirds requirement for earmarked local taxes has been part of California law since Proposition 13 and Proposition 218, and the measure keeps the initiative power from bypassing it.
It is prospective and narrow. Unlike the withdrawn initiative, it does not invalidate existing taxes or add new limits on real estate transfer taxes, which reduces the risk of disruptively unwinding revenue already budgeted.
It adds certainty. Litigation since Upland left the majority-versus-two-thirds question unsettled for years, and a clear constitutional rule would end that ambiguity.
Potential risks
It makes it harder to fund local services. The Legislative Analyst finds local tax revenues could be lower than they otherwise would be, though the size of the effect is unknown.
It lets a minority block a majority. A tax with 60 percent support would fail, so about one-third of voters could defeat a measure the majority favors.
It narrows a core democratic tool. The citizen initiative was designed to let voters act when their elected officials will not, and the measure raises the bar specifically for that path.
Real recent examples would have failed. Several county special taxes for fire, health, and open space passed with majorities below two-thirds and would not have survived this rule.
The ad valorem provision is easy to overlook. Most coverage focuses on the vote threshold, yet the measure also writes a real property tax limit into the constitution, and its practical reach deserves scrutiny.
6. Open questions
How many recent local special taxes actually passed with between a majority and two-thirds vote, and how much revenue statewide would have been at stake under the new rule?
Does the ad valorem provision in subdivision (b) change anything on the ground, or does it mainly codify limits that courts already enforced?
Will the narrower ACA 22 satisfy the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association over time, or does the withdrawn initiative signal a broader effort to come?
How will the measure interact with the exceptions it cross-references in Article XIII C and Article XIII D, and which taxes fall inside or outside those carve-outs?
With the author now opposed to her own measure, how will the yes and no campaigns be organized and funded?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
A special tax funds one specific thing, and the state constitution has long asked for two-thirds approval before a city or county can levy one. Should the same two-thirds rule apply when voters put that tax on the ballot themselves, or should the citizen initiative be a path to a simple-majority tax that elected officials could not pass on their own?
Ask which risk worries you more: A supermajority rule that lets one-third of voters block services the majority wants, or a majority rule that lets an organized campaign commit a community to a targeted tax with less consensus than the constitution otherwise requires?

Requires a Two-Thirds Vote to Approve Local Special Tax Initiatives
PROP
43 Purpose
Proposition 43 is a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature that would raise the
vote share required to enact special tax initiatives proposed by citizens from a simple majority
to a two-thirds majority.1
CALIFORNIA
Research Assistant: Kahani Malhotra ’27
Background
In 1978, California voters passed Proposition 13, requiring that any special tax proposed by a
local government must receive a two-thirds vote from the electorate before being enacted,2
with a special tax being defined as any tax imposed for a specific purpose rather than general
governmental need.3 In 1996, Proposition 218 further increased the power of voters to approve
taxes by requiring that any general tax imposed by a local government must receive majority
voter approval, and reaffirmed that special taxes require two-thirds voter approval.4
Two decades later, a court decision narrowed the scope of Proposition 218. In 2017, the
California Supreme Court ruled in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland that a significant
requirement for general taxes — that they be placed on the ballot during general elections —
did not apply to citizen initiatives.5 Ultimately, the court categorized taxes imposed by local
governments as different from taxes imposed by citizen initiatives.
The ruling raised an important question: Are special taxes imposed by citizen initiatives exempt
from the two-thirds vote requirement that applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local
governments? A memo from the San Francisco attorney’s office interpreting the ruling seemed
to indicate that the answer was yes.6 But the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association disagreed.
In 2018, the Association sued San Francisco for allowing two separate citizen-driven measures
to pass with a simple-majority vote rather than a supermajority vote. A judge ruled against the
Association, affirming that the special tax measures were rightfully passed by majority vote
since they were proposed by citizens.7 A state appeals court shot down the Association’s further
attempts to overturn citizen-initiated local taxes passed in 20208 and 2021.9
In 2023, the Association and the California Business Roundtable qualified an initiative10 for the
2024 ballot cycle that would have mandated any special tax initiative to require a two-thirds
majority vote regardless of whether a local government or citizens proposed it.11 But in June
2024, the California Supreme Court ruled unanimously that passage of the initiative would lead
to a “revision,” rather than an amendment, of the state constitution, “based on its far-reaching
changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained at the
state and local levels.” While amendments may be made by citizen initiatives, revisions require
“a constitutional convention and popular ratification.”12 Thus, enacting the proposal by initiative
would be unconstitutional.
In 2026, the same two organizations qualified an initiative for the 2026 general election
ballot that would have amended the state constitution to require a two-thirds majority to pass
citizen-led local special tax initiatives, alongside other tax limiting provisions.13 Following a
legislative compromise, which included the passage of ACA 22,14 the organizations withdrew the
initiative in favor of Proposition 43 being placed on this year’s ballot as a legislatively referred
constitutional amendment.15 Though ACA 22 passed nearly unanimously in the Assembly (68-2)
and Senate (35-1), its author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-14), announced on June 29 that
she was “adamantly opposed to it.16
Proposal
Proposition 43 would amend the
California Constitution to require that
citizen-driven special tax initiatives
require a two-thirds majority vote
for passage. It would add Section
4.5 to Article XIII A of the California
Constitution, detailing that any local
government — including voters
within a local government exercising
the initiative power — must obtain
a two-thirds vote to enact, extend,
or increase a special tax starting on
January 1, 2027.
The amendment also prohibits local
government and members of the
electorate from levying ad valorem
property taxes — taxes based on the
value of real estate or tangible per-
sonal property — except for certain
preapproved, dedicated property
taxes, whose terms are delineated in
the Constitution.17
Fiscal Impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s
Office (LAO) estimates that Propo-
sition 43 would reduce local govern-
ment tax revenues. The total fiscal
impact is largely unknown, however,
as it depends on future decisions by
voters and local governments.18

Bay Area officials are sounding the alarm over a lesser-known California ballot measure
By Kathryn Palmer (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/kathryn-palmer/) , Staff Writer Oct 12, 2026
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie appears alongside first responders to oppose Proposition 43 outside of Fire Station No. 5 on Oct. 7.
Weston Turtle Fudge/S.F. Chronicle
It’s not often that the supporters and opponents of a ballot measure agree on what exactly it would do, let alone describe it the same way. Yet both sides of the fight over Proposition 43 have been clear: It will make it harder to raise local taxes.
What they don’t agree on is whether it’s a good idea.
Bay Area leaders last week joined a growing chorus of local government officials across the state voicing strong opposition to Proposition 43, slamming the measure as a threat to critical financial lifelines for cities and counties.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Gov. Gavin Newsom on Friday also said he plans to vote against Prop 43, siding with a wide collection of Democratic lawmakers and local government officials who oppose the measure.
Supporters, led by the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, argue that as the state and nation grapple with an affordability crisis, raising taxes should be difficult.
General taxes, which aren’t earmarked for a specific use and go into a city’s general fund, can pass with a simple majority. But taxes that will go toward a specific purpose — like pay raises for police and fire personnel, or homeless services — are subject to a much higher two-thirds vote requirement when they’re placed on the ballot by government officials.
This puts anyone looking to raise revenue in a strange bind: Voters are much more likely to support a tax increase when they know it’s going to fix a specific problem. They’re less likely to OK a general tax hike that could fund virtually anything. Yet the two-thirds requirement is a significant hurdle, making it almost impossible to raise special taxes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 43 would extend that two-thirds threshold to special tax measures placed on the ballot by citizen initiatives, not just those spearheaded by government officials. It would mean all special taxes would need to be approved by a much higher percentage of voters than other ballot measures.
Local leaders across California, including many in the Bay Area, have begun sounding the alarm over the implications if Prop 43 were to pass.
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie, and Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee joined San Francisco Supervisor Bilal Mahmood and representatives of housing and public safety groups last week to urge voters to reject the measure, warning it would hamstring communities’ ability to raise funds for local needs. They also warned that it would enhance the veto power of a select few, potentially inviting “special interests” to try to sway election outcomes.
“Prop 43 undermines democracy by upending majority rule, making it harder for communities across California to support first responders, parks, libraries and affordable housing,” Lurie said at a press conference in San Francisco last week. “Voters know what our communities need to keep our neighborhoods safe, keep Muni moving, and build more housing.”
Supporters have cast the court decisions allowing citizens’ special tax initiatives to pass by simple majority as a loophole. If Prop 43 passes, it would essentially hit the rewind button to a period before a 2017 state Supreme Court decision led to the current simple majority rule.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association spokesperson Susan Shelley said local governments would still be able to pass general tax increases by a simple majority under Prop 43, and argued local officials should prioritize their budgets to pay for essential services first.
“Proposition 43 makes it harder to raise taxes, like sales taxes,” Shelley said. “It restores the requirement for a two-thirds vote of the people if the money from a local tax will be earmarked and locked for a special purpose.”
Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee, third from left, appears in San Francisco alongside first responders to oppose Proposition 43.
Weston Turtle Fudge/S.F. Chronicle The ballot measure also counts Reform California as a supporter, the campaign group helmed by firebrand GOP Assembly Member Carl DeMaio.
The California Republican Party, along with some Republican lawmakers and a few current and former Bay Area officials, back the measure. The list includes Debora Allen, former BART director, and Quentin Kopp, former San Francisco supervisor.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
The coalition of those fighting Prop 43 got a boost last week when Newsom endorsed a no vote, a position in lockstep with the California Democratic Party, several prominent Democratic state and local lawmakers, and associations representing California cities and counties.
The League of California Cities opposes Prop 43, as does the California State Association of Counties and the California Special Districts Association, collectively representing hundreds of municipalities across the state.
Susan Ellenberg, president of the California State Association of Counties, said in a statement to the Chronicle that many local needs depend on community-driven funding, such as wildfire prevention, emergency response and behavioral health.
“The measure would also limit residents’ ability to propose and approve solutions through the initiative process, even when those solutions earn broad majority support,” said Ellenberg, who is also a Santa Clara County supervisor. “For local governments already facing strained budgets and increasing responsibilities, this change would reshape how communities address their most pressing priorities.”
Ellenberg and other Santa Clara County leaders backed a 2024 tax increase that they billed as a measure to fund healthcare services in the wake of Trump administration cuts. But Measure A was a general tax increase, subject to the much lower vote threshold, meaning the money can technically be spent on anything. It passed with 57% of the vote.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
As of Tuesday, the Yes on 43 campaign has a slight financial edge, banking more than $10 million in campaign funds so far. The anti-43 campaign reported just under $8 million.
In 2024, eight special sales tax measures qualified for local ballots across the state by a citizens initiative, with increases ranging from one-fourth of a cent to 1 cent. Of the four that passed with a simple majority, none met Prop 43’s two-thirds vote threshold. The two that received the most support were Sonoma County’s Measure I to fund childcare and Benicia’s Measure F to fund road improvements. They passed at 62% and 61%, respectively.
Other prominent special tax measures include the Los Angeles mansion tax, which voters passed by majority in 2022 and places a 4% tax on real estate sales on multimillion-dollar homes.
Prop 43 arose out of a deal cut to avoid another qualified ballot measure from the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association that took aim at elements of the mansion tax.
It was that last-minute legislative brokering that led the anti-tax group to instead put forward Prop 43, with the help of Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland. Soon after Prop 43 qualified for the November ballot, Wicks disavowed it, calling it “the only path left to get the more dangerous initiative off the ballot.”
Isaac Martin, a sociology professor at UC San Diego who has written multiple books about taxation and public finance, described Prop 43 as affecting a Goldilocks-like subset of tax measures: popular enough for a simple majority, but not popular enough to pass overwhelmingly.
“Since it would make it harder for local governments to raise money for popular services, the options are to raise funds for general government, including popular and less popular services, or do without,” Martin said. “I mean, bottom line, those are sort of the only options for local governments.”
Groups that oppose the measure argue the new threshold would make it harder for communities to make hyper-specific funding decisions to tackle local priorities.
Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters advocacy group representing thousands of firefighters, said the measure risks cutting off crucial public safety funding. He pointed to Measure H in Sonoma County and Measure E in Los Angeles County, both passed by voters in 2024. Both taxes raise funds to bolster the two counties’ fire protection and emergency response services — top priorities in regions that have been devastated by some of the state’s deadliest wildfires in recent years.
“Any time you have local elected leaders, public safety and community advocates, or people that are running local health clinics or infrastructure projects, say that they need to get something done in their community, it should be the community that decides, with a simple majority,” Roberts said.

I'm lining up the next research steps: pulling the editorial endorsements for and against, checking polling on Prop 43, and looking at the Wicks thread on why a "no" vote still makes sense now that the HJTA initiative has been withdrawn.

I'm now checking whether a "no" vote carries any risk, such as HJTA returning with another initiative in 2028, and then looking at how the ad valorem tax provision would affect local taxes, including which November 2026 measures would fall outside its January 2027 start.

I'm weighing whether to give a recommendation at all, since this is a contested ballot question where the answer turns on values about tax thresholds and local services, and I'm also reviewing how the supermajority rules have played out for school bonds and local taxes.

I'm weighing whether to give a bare yes or no, since this is a contested tax question that depends on personal values rather than facts I can settle. I'm leaning toward explaining what a yes vote and a no vote each mean, who backs each side, and the main trade-off, so the user can decide for themselves.

I'm checking whether there's anything objectively verifiable here that would point clearly one way for this user, even though the core choice is a values question about tax thresholds and local services.

I'm weighing whether I can give a conditional answer instead of a bare yes or no: lower taxes points to yes, while keeping local funding flexible points to no. I'm leaning toward briefly explaining that a one-word pick would be a political endorsement, then laying out what each choice means so the user can decide.

I'm checking the factual details that would help the user decide: the measure only reaches citizen-initiative special taxes, general taxes are unaffected, and it applies only prospectively from January 1, 2027. A "no" vote keeps the status quo, and the broader HJTA initiative is already withdrawn, though HJTA could return in a future cycle. I'm also noting the fiscal uncertainty the LAO flagged and the 2024 precedent, where several citizen special taxes won majorities but none reached two-thirds.

I'm checking the transfer-tax claims in the arguments against what Prop 43 actually does, since the cap that was in the withdrawn initiative doesn't appear in this measure.

I'm checking the ballot argument against the measure text: the "No" side says Prop 43 doesn't cut taxes, which holds, but the Yes side's claims about spending restrictions and voter rights aren't in the text. Those claims need a closer look before I weigh either side.

I'm noting that local governments can still pass general taxes by simple majority, and that citizen-initiated general taxes aren't affected by Prop 43, which only reaches special taxes. I also want to confirm the LAO's point that voter-proposed new, increased, or extended special taxes would need two-thirds, and that a "No" vote keeps the current majority threshold for those initiatives.

I'm dropping the Fresno transport tax idea as not needed, and now I'm looking for polling on Prop 43, starting with the PPIC survey and the Berkeley IGS poll.
